items.body:
## Summary

The ChatGPT desktop app's local Codex chat repeatedly crashed when opening one existing thread. That thread had a persisted right-panel preview tab for a large, image-heavy PDF. Temporarily making that PDF unavailable allowed the thread to open. After closing the PDF preview tab and restoring the original PDF file, reopening the same thread succeeded without another crash during a short observation period.

The PDF preview is the leading suspected trigger based on isolation, not a confirmed internal root cause. We have not tested this with an unrelated PDF or a clean new thread.

## Environment

- ChatGPT desktop app on macOS, bundle ID `com.openai.codex`
- App version: `26.1013.40934`, build `20770`
- macOS: `26.5.2 (25F84)`
- Architecture: Apple Silicon / ARM64
- Codex Framework version in the crash report path: `155.0.8059.80`
- Incident date: October 19, 2026; times below are UTC+08:00
- Local, existing Codex thread
- PDF: 231,393,788 bytes (~220.7 MiB), 148 pages, mostly illustrated comic pages

## Reproduction observed on this machine

1. A local Codex thread had previously opened the PDF with `open_in_codex` as a file preview.
2. The PDF tab remained saved in that thread's right-panel tab state.
3. Open that thread again from the sidebar, including after restarting the desktop app.
4. The app restores the PDF preview and the entire desktop app exits shortly afterwards, rather than only the PDF pane failing.

The initial opening of the PDF and the precise internal crash point were not captured. The repeatedly observed trigger was reopening the existing thread with the saved PDF preview.

## Actual behavior

Repeated whole-app exits. There were eight macOS `.ips` reports between 13:44 and 13:49, and additional reports at 13:55:41 and 13:56:22 after an initial transcript-size repair attempt.

The inspected reports show:

- Process: `ChatGPT`
- Faulting thread: main thread / `CrBrowserMain`
- Exception: `EXC_BREAKPOINT`, signal `SIGTRAP`
- Termination: signal 5 / `Trace/BPT trap: 5`
- The first two stack frames are in Codex Framework at image offsets `74827220` and `74827112`; the next two are at `101244724` and `101244604`.

The symbol names in the reports have very large symbol displacements, so they should not be treated as reliable function-level attribution. The application logs immediately before the crashes show thread loading/resuming and history item reads. In one of the later attempts, navigation and resume were logged as successful before the process exited.

## Isolation and workaround

The following troubleshooting was performed in order, with backups:

1. The thread originally had a ~438 MB JSONL transcript and ~187 MB of inline image data in its history projection. One truncated JSONL record also had a complete successor with the same call ID.
2. A repair externalized inline images to existing/local image files, removed the truncated duplicate, and rebuilt this thread's history projection. The transcript fell to ~4.85 MB and backend history reads started succeeding. **The desktop app still crashed when opening the thread.**
3. Inspection of the saved UI state showed the 231,393,788-byte PDF was still the active right-panel artifact tab.
4. Temporarily renaming only that PDF prevented its preview from loading. The thread could then be opened and its history read successfully, with no new crash report during observation.
5. The user closed the PDF tab. The saved tab routes for that thread became empty.
6. The PDF was restored to its original name, with matching SHA-256 before/after. The same thread was reopened successfully. After 15 seconds, backend history reads still succeeded and there was no newer crash report.

The initial transcript repair is a confounding change relative to the original state, but the crash still occurred after that change and stopped only after disabling/restoring the PDF preview as described. Closing the persisted PDF tab is the effective workaround observed here.

## Expected behavior

Restoring a saved PDF preview should not terminate the entire application. If a PDF exceeds supported resource/IPC limits or cannot be previewed, show an error or size limit in the preview pane and keep the chat usable. A failed preview should not create a repeated crash loop when reopening the chat.

## Requested investigation

Please investigate the desktop main-process PDF loading/transport path and persisted artifact-tab restoration for large PDFs. A recoverable error and a way to reopen a thread without restoring a problematic preview would prevent this crash loop.

This report intentionally omits full conversation content, user file paths, and the PDF itself. Original crash reports and diagnostic data are retained locally and can be provided privately if needed.

items.title: Windows Computer Use: locale-sensitive Document selection, same-host language retest, and residual en-US failure

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary

Windows Computer Use repeatedly stopped while reading Chrome state on my `zh-CN` Windows session. After I changed the Windows display language to English, the same installed helper successfully returned Chrome accessibility text and a screenshot. The successful accessibility output contained `document`, `ID: RootWebArea`, and a nonempty HTTPS URL.

A read-only inspection of the installed helper identifies a locale-sensitive predicate: it prefers UIA's localized control-type string as the internal role, then compares that role with ASCII `document`. A separate UIA probe run through Claude Code recorded `文档` on this machine.

**Scope:** this confirms the predicate defect and adds same-machine runtime evidence supporting the language-related explanation. It does not identify the exact rejected node in the original Chrome failure. A later operation in the English session also returned the same error, so switching to English did not eliminate every occurrence.

## Relationship to existing reports

This is a follow-up evidence report for [#25271](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/25271), [#45996](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/45996), [#53026](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/53026), [#54458](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/54458), and especially [#54532](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/54532).

The following are already reported and are **not new discoveries** here:

- [#25271, comment 5558273508](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/25271#issuecomment-5558273508) reports that changing only the browser language did not help, while changing Windows display language to English did.
- [#54532, comment 6232015995](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/54532#issuecomment-6232015995) already discusses the localized-role mechanism, the same helper hash, and UIA properties.
- English-language failures also already appear in [#25271, comment 5618209961](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/25271#issuecomment-5618209961).

The additional evidence here is:

1. Timestamped failure and success through the supported `@oai/sky` API on this machine, with an unchanged signed helper hash.
2. Separate successful text-only and screenshot-only reads after the language change, including the actual formatted document role, ID, and URL-presence result.
3. A local re-verification of the already reported binary mechanism, extending the checked path through candidate rejection to the exact error dispatcher, with SDK vtable mapping and instruction-byte verification.
4. Reviewable UIA probe results, with the important distinction that the complete property tuple came from Chromium-based desktop applications rather than the original failing Chrome page.
5. A subsequent English-session failure, preserved separately to avoid presenting the workaround as a complete fix.

## Environment

| Component | Observed version/state |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | Windows 11 Pro 25H2, build 26200.9711 |
| Codex Desktop MSIX | 26.1013.4894.0 |
| Bundled `@oai/sky` | 0.7.8 |
| Chrome file version | 155.0.8059.80 |
| Windows UI culture before / after | `zh-CN` / `en-US` |
| Native helper | `codex-computer-use.exe`, 1,551,152 bytes |
| Authenticode | Valid, OpenAI OpCo, LLC |

Helper SHA-256, identical before and after the successful language retest:

```text
B6B0E4979B89E5C22DAB866F0974BC817C0D08CB359E1C2DD7BE3DCCB9E181EB
```

The binary was not patched for these tests.

## Supported-API observations before and after the language change

All timestamps below are UTC on **2026-10-19**.

| Time | Session | Operation | Observed result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 04:09:38.727 | `zh-CN` | `get_window_state({include_screenshot:false, include_text:true})` after separate successful `list_apps` and `get_window` calls | Exact URL-confidence stop below; no accessibility tree returned |
| 05:43:07.715–05:43:08.964 | `en-US` | Same text-only state-read options on the current Chrome window | Success; 2,338-character accessibility tree |
| 05:43:25.832–05:43:26.028 | `en-US` | `get_window_state({include_screenshot:true, include_text:false})` | Success; displayed 1536 × 960 screenshot |
| 05:46:20.648 | Same English session | One cell containing `press_key(Alt_L+Return)` followed by a text-only state read | Same URL-confidence stop; failing sub-call and resulting page state unknown |

The successful formatted tree included this redacted line:

```text
11 document [page title omitted] Value: https://[page URL omitted] ID: RootWebArea
```

The actual URL was nonempty; the redactions above remove unrelated browsing details. This was the official formatted accessibility output, not a fresh raw UIA-property capture.

Exact error:

```text
Computer Use has been stopped for this turn because it could not determine the current browser URL on Windows with enough confidence to enforce policy. Stop your work and send a final message noting why Computer Use ended.
```

The initial isolated state-read failure returned `isError:true`, execution duration 27 ms, and `codex/telemetry.error_code:"unknown"`. The later English-session failure returned the same fields with a 116 ms execution duration. Neither response exposed the native candidate, rejection stage, confidence value, rule ID, or native request ID.

The language comparison is observational: the desktop session, window handles, and page state also changed. It is not a controlled single-variable A/B test.

### Remaining failure in the English session

While preparing this report, Chrome accessibility reads continued to work. Focusing the address bar with Ctrl+L and entering `https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/new/choose` each succeeded with a subsequent state read. The next cell was:

```js
await sky.press_key({ window, key: "Alt_L+Return" });
await sky.get_window_state({
  window,
  include_screenshot: false,
  include_text: true
});
```

That cell returned the same stop message. There was no success marker between the two calls, so the trace does not establish whether input completed or which sub-call failed. Computer Use was stopped after the response. The target page was not inspected afterward. I cannot attribute this occurrence to a blank tab, navigation transition, missing property, or the localized-role predicate.

## UIA probe results and their limits

Claude Code separately ran a read-only PowerShell/.NET UIA probe in the desktop session. It enumerated `Chrome_WidgetWin_1` windows, selected descendants by numeric Document control type, and read `.Current` properties plus `ValuePattern.Current.Value`.

At 04:48:45–04:48:46, the probe recorded:

| Host process / document | ControlType | LocalizedControlType | AutomationId | ValuePattern value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude desktop, document 1 | 50030 / Document | `文档` | `RootWebArea` | Nonempty, length 137 |
| Claude desktop, document 2 | 50030 / Document | `文档` | `RootWebArea` | Nonempty, length 59 |
| ChatGPT desktop process | 50030 / Document | `文档` | `RootWebArea` | Nonempty, length 18 |
| Discord | 50030 / Document | `文档` | `RootWebArea` | Nonempty, length 51 |

All four reported `FrameworkId="Chrome"`. The localized string's code points were U+6587 and U+6863.

A second probe set its own process/thread preferred UI languages to `en-US`; both setter calls returned true, and the thread preference read back as `en-US`. These nodes still returned `文档`. This only establishes the result of that client-process experiment; it does not establish the complete Windows language-resource resolution path.

Two later JSON captures at 05:23:33 and 05:23:38 showed the same complete tuples for documents in those Chromium-based desktop applications. Across the four captures, a Chrome window containing an `OmniboxViewViews` control exposed no Document node to this probe; a separate Chrome WebView document exposed `文档` but had an empty AutomationId and an unsupported ValuePattern.

Consequently, these captures do **not** expose the original rejected Chrome root node. They establish that this machine supplies localized Document labels on real Chromium-hosted nodes with otherwise usable IDs and values. The probe reads current properties; the helper path below uses cached properties. The probe's calculated selector booleans are a simulation, not native helper tracing.

## Installed-helper code evidence

This is bounded disassembly of the installed signed binary, not source code from the public repository. Addresses below are RVAs for the hash above.

| Location | Observed behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `0x2052B` | Calls UIA vtable offset `0x1B0`, identified from the Windows SDK as `get_CachedLocalizedControlType` (zero-based slot 54). A successful nonempty string becomes the internal role. |
| Role fallback | Numeric `get_CachedControlType` at `0x1A8` / slot 53 is used only when the localized getter fails or returns empty. The fallback maps 50030 to `document`. |
| `0x1C2D6` / `0x1C2E3` | Candidate selection loads the ASCII `document` literal at the first address and calls the comparator at the second. It uses an equal-length, ASCII case-insensitive comparison. A nonempty `文档` fails this predicate without reaching the numeric fallback. |
| Subsequent predicates | The trimmed `CachedAutomationId` must match `rootwebarea`; the selected value must be nonempty after trimming. The getter is `get_CachedAutomationId` at `0x1E8` / slot 61, not `CachedAriaRole`. |
| No-candidate dispatch | The Chrome/Edge/Brave/Opera path produces tag `0x8000000000000002`. Jump-table index 2 resolves to `0x7754B`, which loads the exact error above before the later URL-classification/network-verification path. |

The SDK mapping was checked against Windows SDK 10.0.26100.0. Across eight bounded disassembly extracts, the encoded bytes of 735 disassembled instructions were checked against the original executable; all matched. This validates the extracted bytes and supports the static interpretation, but is not an execution trace of either failed call.

Microsoft documents [Document's numeric identifier as 50030](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winauto/uiauto-controltype-ids) and distinguishes the localized control-type description from [UIA's other element properties](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winauto/uiauto-automation-element-propids).

## Expected behavior and requested investigation

Document recognition should use the locale-independent numeric control type rather than an English comparison against a localized display string, while retaining the existing URL validation and policy checks.

Please consider:

- A locale-independent Document predicate, with regression coverage for English and non-English UIA labels.
- Separate coverage for stable pages, new-tab/navigation states, absent root nodes, missing values, and missing AutomationId.
- Supported, privacy-preserving diagnostics for candidate count, numeric control type, localized role, ID/value presence, getter failures, and the candidate-rejection stage.

The static defect is actionable, and the same-host language retest supports its practical relevance. Exact attribution of the original Chrome failure and the later English-session failure still requires native per-request diagnostics. No patched or upstream source-level fix was tested in this investigation.

items.title: Windows Full access blocks authorized file cleanup without an approval path; use Auto-review or restore previous behavior

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Installed Windows Appx package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1013.4894.0`.
Bundled/running CLI: `0.163.0-alpha.10.2`, verified from the executable and session metadata.
The About dialog was not independently checked.

### What subscription do you have?

Not provided.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11, build 26300.
PowerShell 7.7.0-preview.5, invoked through its real executable path.

### What issue are you seeing?

The desktop app's **Full access** preset can reject explicitly authorized cleanup of project-owned temporary files before PowerShell starts, returning only `blocked by policy`. There is no approval dialog, useful rejection rationale, or supported way to authorize the operation in the conversation.

In my experience, earlier versions' Full access allowed this routine cleanup. I have not identified the first affected version, so the regression range is unknown.

The practical failure is: **Codex cannot delete its temporary files, does not offer an approval window, and leaves the user to delete files manually or investigate/edit configuration.** A permission preset intended for unattended work should provide a complete, understandable authorization path.

### Recorded incidents

Two independently recorded tool rejections on October 19, 2026:

| UTC time | Operation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 00:26:26.991Z | Cleanup of 19 interrupted-test temporary directories using `Remove-Item -LiteralPath ... -Recurse -Force` | Rejected before process creation; nothing deleted |
| 01:12:50.685Z | Non-recursive deletion of one ordinary 110-byte lock file, after its owning process had exited | Rejected before process creation; user later deleted it manually |

The effective turn context for **both** incidents was:

```json
{
  "approval_policy": "never",
  "approvals_reviewer": "user",
  "sandbox_policy": { "type": "danger-full-access" }
}
```

Both commands used the PowerShell 7 executable directly, without `cmd /c` or a `require_escalated` request. The lock-file operation was an exact single-file deletion, not recursive cleanup.

The tool returned a CreateProcess rejection containing:

```text
rejected: blocked by policy
```

It supplied no policy source, matched rule, reviewer identifier, rationale, or recovery instruction. Because PowerShell never started, this is not an observed PowerShell ACL/file-in-use error. These historical incidents also **cannot be attributed to Auto-review**: their recorded reviewer was `user`.

Diagnostic call IDs:

- `call_3d6ad2b4e04e45feb52c20007ae0d859`
- `call_2954353d5fc444dc81f74386cae7fd8c`

### Impact on a real cleanup workflow

A separate repository-cleanup conversation documented an accumulation of old builds, candidates, caches, and temporary material. It eventually cleaned **623 targets covering 3,250,853 logical files and approximately 175.9 GiB of file lengths**, including 175 old scripts.

However, cleanup of the cleanup task's own **six remaining helper files, approximately 0.84 MiB**, was still rejected with the same generic policy message, including a non-recursive command listing six absolute literal paths.

This demonstrates that large cleanup can succeed while narrowly scoped final cleanup remains blocked without an explanation. The 175.9 GiB figure is aggregate logical file size, not measured physical space reclaimed; I am not claiming that all of this accumulation was caused by these policy rejections.

### Configuration and UI ambiguity

My intended defaults in `config.toml` are:

```toml
sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"
approval_policy = "on-request"
approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"
```

The [sandboxing documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing) describes the UI Full access preset as `danger-full-access + never`, while [Auto-review documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing/auto-review) explains that Auto-review handles requests that would otherwise require interactive approval. With `never`, there are no such approval requests to review.

A conversation-level Full access preset overriding file defaults could therefore explain why my intended Auto-review configuration was not active. **This precedence explanation is a hypothesis, not a verified cause of the deletion rejection.** The inspected config file's modification time was later than the two historical incidents, so its current contents do not independently establish its exact contents at those times.

The resulting UX requires users to understand the distinction between Full access, Custom/config defaults, approval policy, reviewer selection, and additional undisclosed enforcement.

### Requested behavior / two proposed solutions

Please consider either of these product-level solutions:

1. **Make the UI Full access preset use `danger-full-access + on-request + auto_review`.** This would give broad access while routing approval requests to Auto-review, allowing approved routine operations to proceed without manual approval dialogs or manual config editing.
2. **Restore the previous Full access behavior for explicitly authorized operations**, so routine, bounded cleanup of disposable project files can complete as it did in earlier versions.

The first proposal does not assume Auto-review can override a separate hard policy denial. If an additional enforcement layer caused these incidents, that layer also needs a fix or a supported authorization path; changing the preset alone may not resolve it.

If an action must remain blocked, please show the actual policy source and rationale and provide an actionable resolution. A silent dead end with neither execution nor approval is the core problem.

Please also display the **effective** sandbox mode, approval policy, reviewer, and their configuration sources in the UI so users can see when a conversation preset overrides their defaults.

### Local investigation and limitations

- Inspected user rules contained 72 allow entries and no explicit forbidden/prompt entries; 10 mentioned `Remove-Item`. Exact argv matching was not tested.
- No relevant project/ancestor `.codex/config.toml` or project rules were found.
- The inspected local managed-configuration locations were absent.
- These observations do not exclude built-in policies, remote requirements, or another enforcement layer.
- A later context changed the reviewer to `auto_review`; no new deletion test was performed after that change, so it is not a verified fix.
- No new deletion reproduction, permission modification, or alternative-tool workaround was attempted for this report.

### Questions for maintainers

1. Which policy/enforcement path can reject these commands before process creation under the recorded Full access context?
2. Is this intended enforcement, a false positive, or a permission/configuration propagation defect?
3. If Full access cannot authorize routine temporary-file cleanup, what supported UI workflow should users use without manual config editing?
4. Can the app expose both effective permission sources and the precise reason for a rejection?

### Reproduction status

These are observed incidents with recorded effective contexts, not a newly executed minimal reproduction. The operational sequence was: select Full access, explicitly authorize cleanup of disposable project files, and let Codex issue the bounded PowerShell deletion command. The tool rejected it before process creation without an approval route.

Private project paths, full configuration, credentials, raw transcripts, and file contents are omitted.

Related reports: #54610, #54746, #52966. This report adds exact single-file evidence, the cleanup-workflow impact, and the specific request to fix the desktop permission preset/approval experience.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### Environment

- Official Codex 0.163.0, x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, Ubuntu 24.04 / WSL2 kernel 6.6.87.2.
- Shared managed app-server and code-mode host. Default sandbox launches intermittently fail before the command runs; an earlier explicit host launch also failed.
- Tool errors include `Failed to create unified exec process: No file descriptors available (os error 24)` and failure to spawn the code-mode host with the same errno. There is no child exit code when creation fails.
- A documented same-version daemon restart did not reliably remove the symptom. No permanent FD-limit, ptrace-policy, package, or authentication changes were applied in the current investigation.

### Retained failure trace: 2026-10-18 21:18:41.520783–21:19:51.914777 UTC

A previously retained strace file contains 72,192 EMFILE returns. TID 433 accounts for:

- 71,983 `pipe2(pointer, 0x80000) = -1 EMFILE` returns; `0x80000` matches `O_CLOEXEC` on this Linux host.
- 49 `open` EMFILE returns.

Other TIDs also report open/openat/socket EMFILE returns. This is a retained syscall trace, not just the application's error string. The repeated pipe failures are about 1,000 per second during this window.

The contemporaneous application logs identify a Codex daemon process and os-error-24 reports in:

- `codex_skills_extension::host_service`, `ext/skills/src/host_service.rs:414`;
- `codex_skills_extension::loader::host`, `ext/skills/src/loader/host.rs:184`;
- `codex_thread_store::local::live_writer`, `thread-store/src/local/live_writer.rs:363`;
- `codex_core::session`, `core/src/session/mod.rs:2689`.

The TID-to-TGID mapping at that historical failure was not independently retained. Application-log correlation is by time, not proof that all listed TIDs shared that daemon's FD table.

### Important limits

The three later retained traces inspected here contain no successful syscall returns. They cannot reconstruct FD allocations versus closes, and their original invocation flags have not been established. No allocation stack or failure-instant FD inventory/limit was retained. The old TID is no longer present in the host process namespace.

An earlier, separate 45-second trace had zero parsed EMFILE events but discarded 22 undecoded lines and did not fully account for trailing data. That older negative result is explicitly incomplete.

During successful windows, daemon FD counts were 63–72 against soft/hard NOFILE 10240/1048576. A sparse high FD number was seen earlier; that is not a count of open FDs. These measurements do not describe the historical failure instant.

### Additional controlled observations, 2026-10-19

- A current daemon process also logged os error 24 at 03:56:29 UTC; recurrence is not limited to the previous daemon identity.
- One 45-second, non-ptrace host FD observation collected 1,946 samples. Daemon leader peak was 67; sampled daemon-thread peak was 61; code-mode-host peak was 9. One normal sandboxed printf launch succeeded. This did not reproduce failure or establish a fix.
- A separate, one-shot 45-second strace capture was attached to the exact current daemon and code-mode-host identities. It selected failed pipe/pipe2 calls with stacks, used a bounded metadata-only parser, and made one ordinary sandboxed launch. That launch succeeded; zero selected pipe failures occurred. Both processes retained their identity and TracerPid returned to zero. No application process was restarted or terminated.
- Matching official 0.163.0 debug-symbol assets were downloaded and their SHA-256 checked. GNU debuglink CRCs matched both installed binaries. The downloaded symbols were not executed or installed over the active binaries.

### Request

Please identify the likely pipe-allocation/retry path for this version and advise a bounded way to capture the allocating stack and the failing thread's actual FD table/NOFILE limit without losing the failure to ptrace timing effects. Is there a known fix for this specific Linux/musl managed-daemon symptom?

We have not established a persistent FD leak, the source of descriptor consumption, a lower failure-time limit, or a bubblewrap/shell defect. Raising limits, disabling plugins, or upgrading to an unverified build is not presented as a verified repair. Raw traces and private local paths/session identifiers are intentionally omitted.

items.body:
Codex desktop Windows: repeatable read ENOTCONN when selecting one chat

Selecting one particular local chat produces approximately 18 main-process JavaScript error dialogs. The conversation remains usable. The dialogs stop after dismissal and recur after switching away and selecting the chat again. This is the owner's observation; no additional reproduction was performed.

The captured error is Error: read ENOTCONN. Its stack passes through node:net tryReadStart, Socket creation and child_process.spawn, ending at Object.ar with visible column 7687. The installed package is OpenAI.Codex 26.1013.4894.0. The configured updater reports 26.1013.40934, build 20770, prod, up_to_date. Those are separate package/updater version fields. Windows Repair was previously reported ineffective, without independently verified execution/completion.

Static inspection found a strongly matching call site: function ar, exported as et, in .vite/build/application-network-startup-DB1VeU3v.js, native spawn invocation at line 11, column 7687. The process wrapper handles stdin errors by killing an unsettled owned child and forwarding the original error on the child, but lacks corresponding stdout/stderr error handlers for the launcher's piped outputs. Please investigate whether an unhandled output-pipe error is the source of the dialogs and identify the chat-specific triggering child.

A separate-copy candidate extends the same existing guarded error-forwarding behavior to all three child streams. Exactly one expression changed; reverse replacement reproduces the source. Static Node syntax validation passes. The candidate was not runtime-tested, installed, or represented as a confirmed fix. Synchronous spawn failure handling also needs separate review while preserving the returned process API.

Please provide a supported preservation-safe correction or signed application update. No service was stopped or disabled; no sandbox, permission, trust, profile, chat, credential or application installation change was performed. The shared application-package path does not establish sandbox-service causation.

This prepared text includes no local workspace paths, chat identifiers, raw logs, session transcripts, project source, credentials or protected records.

Possibly related prior report: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/43044 . Its workspace conditions and reported mitigation have not been established for this case.

items.title: Windows: Artifact Session host leaves uncancelled shutdown timers, delaying Codex exit ~5s

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary
On Windows, Codex exit is delayed by approximately five seconds. An independently launched, empty Artifact Session host reproduces the delay: its `close()` completes in under 0.4 ms, but the Node.js process stays alive for ~5 seconds. Inspection of the installed `@oai/artifact-tool` package identifies uncancelled `setTimeout` promises used in `Promise.race` during shutdown.

## Environment
- Windows, Codex desktop application (Store installation)
- Codex runtime: `26.1017.11052`, installed 2026-10-18 19:25 JST
- `@oai/artifact-tool`: `2.8.99`
- File: `dist/artifact-session/host-daemon.mjs`
- Installed file SHA-256: `f0c829aa03f2a500a2ece1582c583e9777fdc6cd1549331b0ee62fbac7b27a9a`

## Evidence in the installed implementation
The default shutdown grace is `shutdownGraceMs:5e3` (5,000 ms), passed into shutdown as:
```js
await this.#W(e.graceMs??this.#i.shutdownGraceMs)
```
Shutdown uses:
```js
await Promise.race([Promise.allSettled([...this.#c]),aCt(e)]);
await Promise.race([r,aCt(Math.min(e,1e3))]);
await Promise.race([r,aCt(1e3)]);
```
where:
```js
function aCt(t){return new Promise(e=>setTimeout(e,t))}
```
When the other promise wins, `Promise.race` does not cancel the timeout. No `clearTimeout` or `unref` is used for these timers. Pending timers keep the Node.js event loop alive after `close()` returns.

## Isolated reproduction
Started the bundled `startArtifactSessionHostDaemon` in an independent process with an empty temporary store and a dedicated random local pipe. No Codex instance was connected; no external services, model requests, or user/work data were involved. The installed package was not modified. Both processes exited naturally (code 0, no stderr).

| Shutdown grace | close() duration | Time from close() completion to natural process exit |
|---|---:|---:|
| Default (5,000 ms) | 0.3823 ms | 5,009.8145 ms |
| Explicit 100 ms (test instance only) | 0.3625 ms | 1,002.2727 ms |

The 100-ms test suggests a separate 1-second timer also remains pending; reducing the grace setting alone does not fully resolve the issue.

## Actual Codex exit observation (2026-10-19 JST)
- Codex PID 30700 began exit around 14:17:28.260.
- Most MCP/other children had exited by 14:17:28.31.
- Last Node.js child PID 41556 exited at 14:17:33.230538, exit code 0.
- Codex PID 30700 exited at 14:17:33.311695, exit code 0.
- The Node binary was the bundled runtime `dependencies/node/bin/node.exe`.
- In a subsequent running Codex instance (PID 19676), its sole child using that same Node binary (PID 39060) was running `@oai/artifact-tool/dist/artifact-session/host-daemon.mjs`.

**Attribution caveat:** The command line and stack of the former PID 41556 were not captured. Its identification as the Artifact Session host relies on comparison with the corresponding child of the later instance. The isolated host reproducer independently demonstrates the timer leak.

## Potential regression and user impact
A Windows Store update completed around 2026-10-18 19:25 JST; runtime `26.1017.11052` was installed shortly thereafter. An older runtime `26.1013.11914` was previously available. The older artifact-tool implementation was not retained for comparison, so this is **not yet confirmed as a regression introduced by that update**.

The delayed exit may also widen a race in which a new launch request is delivered to an instance that is shutting down, opening the old window and losing the request. This launch-routing behavior needs separate investigation; the timer leak is the independently reproduced defect.

## Suggested fix
Cancel timeout handles when the competing shutdown operation completes (including failure paths), rather than leaving losing `Promise.race` timers alive. `unref()` could prevent them from blocking process exit, but cancelling them is preferable.

All evidence above was gathered read-only from the installed implementation or from an isolated empty host. No installed libraries, configuration, or environment variables were modified.

### Summary
Windows native Computer Use intermittently returns pixels from a different foreground application. Fresh re-selection and activation restored correct Notepad captures, and standard Notepad keyboard/mouse controls then passed. Earlier Roblox Player calls returned normally but did not produce a confirmed target response. These observations do not establish a shared root cause or a general input failure.

### Environment
- Windows 11 Home, 64-bit, build 26300; NVIDIA RTX 3060.
- Observed installed Windows package: 26.1013.4894.0 (not an app About-dialog version).
- Bundled Computer Use skill: 26.1013.40934.
- Installed @oai/sky metadata at the observed helper runtime path: 0.7.8. A per-call native executor receipt was not available.
- Read-only process checks: the desktop main process, two Codex processes, three Computer Use helper processes, Notepad, and Roblox were all non-elevated, medium-integrity RID 8192, Windows session 1. No elevation or security setting changes were made.

### Actual controls and results
1. Used the documented Node REPL entry point importing @oai/sky. Selected the unique returned Notepad window; never guessed window handles.
2. Created a new blank Notepad tab using Control_L+n. Clicked its editing surface, then press_key with key 2. The document visibly contained 2, and the status bar showed one character.
3. A subsequent click/refresh sequence targeting Notepad returned an image of a Chrome X page instead. We did not act on that unrelated page or save/attach that capture. Whether foreground contention or capture routing caused the mismatch is unknown.
4. Re-enumerated windows, selected the unique Notepad, activated and captured fresh state. The correct Notepad tab containing 2 was visible.
5. In a separate action cell, explicitly activated the same current window and clicked the observed Edit menu using the latest screenshot ID and window-relative coordinates. The Edit menu visibly opened.
6. Explicit activation followed by press_key Escape closed that menu. Thus normal supported keyboard and mouse inputs can work in a standard application.
7. During a separate earlier Roblox Player attempt, the owner entered Adopt Me through the normal official Player and reported that their physical Escape key opened the Roblox menu. Our documented click/press_key calls returned without an error, but the corresponding game UI response was not confirmed after fresh observations. JS reset, window re-selection and activation did not establish successful control. No gameplay activity was completed by the agent.
8. The current Roblox process has no targetable window, so no fresh Roblox comparison has been attempted from that state and no second Player was launched.

### Questions
- What supported diagnostics verify selected-window identity against captured pixels and distinguish foreground loss from capture-routing faults?
- What does successful completion of click/press_key guarantee: event submission or actual target processing? Is there a supported non-sensitive receipt?
- Is Roblox Player or other raw-input game interaction supported by this Windows API, including held-key inputs? The documented press_key surface exposes no duration or separate down/up events.
- Is there a documented fixed build or supported recovery for these symptoms?

### Related reports
- #52981: wrong-window captures and activation problems in Explorer. We have not established the same cause; our Notepad control checks passed after fresh activation.
- #54131: normally returned clicks without a confirmed launcher response. We have not established the same monitor or geometry conditions.

No private paths, process IDs, account names, credentials, screenshots, accessibility dumps, game files, save data, or session transcripts are included in this report. ### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.40934 (About dialog; released October 17, 2026)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex Desktop frequently stops showing visible progress in a local conversation while the thread remains `active` and the latest turn remains `inProgress`. The last visible `commandExecution` completes, but no later assistant message or tool event appears.

On October 19, 2026, a read-only monitor recorded four suspected no-progress periods in one conversation. It detected them after 10m40s–14m47s without an update; the longest lasted about 5h34m after the last recorded command completed. The conversation did not recover on its own. I manually paused it and started a separate, empty conversation; Codex became usable in the new conversation, while the original remained stalled.

This happens frequently enough to make Codex effectively unusable during affected work. I did not encounter this behavior in earlier Codex versions. I do not know the exact first affected app version or the root cause.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. On Codex Desktop for Windows, use a local conversation for normal work that includes one or more tool or command executions.
2. Wait for a visible `commandExecution` to complete, then continue using the same conversation.
3. Observe the conversation’s thread status, latest turn status, and event timestamps. In the affected cases, the thread remained `active` and the latest turn remained `inProgress`, but no newer assistant message or tool event appeared.
4. The monitor detected these no-progress periods after 10m40s–14m47s without an update. This state occurred four times in one monitored conversation; the longest lasted about 5h34m after the last recorded command completed.

The exact prompt, tool, or action that triggers the stall is not yet known, so these steps are an observed sequence rather than a deterministic minimal reproduction.

For recovery, I manually paused the stalled conversation and started a separate, empty conversation. Codex worked in the new conversation, while the original conversation remained stalled. This was a user intervention, not an automatic recovery.

### What is the expected behavior?

After a tool or command completes, the conversation should continue with visible assistant or tool progress, ask me for input, or show a clear error with a safe recovery option. It should not remain `active` / `inProgress` for hours without new messages or tool events. The app should also make the conversation’s actual state clear so I can tell whether it is still working and recover without abandoning the stalled conversation.

### Additional information

A redacted, read-only excerpt from the local desktop log showed successful `thread/resume` and `turn/start` responses in the foreground renderer. Around the same operations, the hidden `avatarOverlay` renderer logged `Conversation state not found` and `turn/started for unknown conversation`. The excerpt also contained at least six `turn/interrupt` → `turn/start` pairs over roughly 19 minutes; it does not show what initiated them.

These logs suggest a possible turn lifecycle or renderer synchronization issue, but do not establish the cause. The monitor could not read CPU, available RAM, or Codex process usage. GPU readings were system-wide and may include other applications.

Potentially related reports to compare: #52529, #47910, and #43525. I am not claiming they have the same root cause. No raw logs, conversation IDs, local paths, or project contents are attached.

Pro.

With **GPT-6 Astra / Ultra** selected for my regular work, the English-language Profile statistic **Most used reasoning** displayed **Extra High · 62%**.

A read-only local audit found that Ultra remains selected in configuration and runtime records, and subagent delegation actually runs. The statistic therefore leaves it unclear whether it represents the user-selected mode or a normalized request-level effort.

The displayed value is transcribed from my observed English UI. The audit did not independently refetch the current server statistic. This report does **not** claim that 62% of tasks were downgraded or that the numerical percentage is demonstrably wrong.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed on my existing account:

1. Use Codex Desktop with **GPT-6 Astra / Ultra** selected for regular tasks.
2. Open the Profile statistics and inspect **Most used reasoning**.
3. Switch the UI to English to distinguish Extra High from Ultra unambiguously.
4. Observe **Extra High · 62%**, despite consistently selecting Ultra.

I have not tested reproduction on a fresh account, and the service's aggregation period is unknown.

### What is the expected behavior?

The statistic should either reflect the user-selected mode (**Ultra**) or explicitly state that it represents normalized request-level reasoning effort and explain how Ultra is represented.

Please also clarify the aggregation period, counting unit/denominator, and whether subagent or background-task requests are included. Without this information, users cannot meaningfully reconcile the statistic with their selected mode.

### Additional information

**Local evidence, audited on 2026-10-19**

- Both the default configuration and recent composer selections preserve `gpt-6-astra` / `ultra`.
- In the seven days ending **2026-10-19 12:33 UTC+08:00**, all **280 user-thread turns** and **613 subagent turns** in the local audit recorded `effort=ultra` and `collaboration_mode.settings.reasoning_effort=ultra`.
- These are unique local turn counts. Inherited history and repeated contexts were deduplicated; the investigation itself and automatic safety-review tasks were excluded. These counts are **not** a reconstruction of the server statistic's denominator.
- Before the investigation, an Astra Ultra parent task launched an Astra Ultra subagent and received its result. This confirms that delegation actually occurred; it does not reveal the backend's internal reasoning budget.

**Possible normalization relationship, not a confirmed root cause**

The installed model catalog gives Astra `multi_agent_reasoning_effort: "xhigh"`. The inspected [public effort-resolution implementation](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/89461ea6833832b0551ce24ee32205824d5c108d/codex-rs/protocol/src/openai_models/reasoning_effort.rs#L9-L35) resolves Ultra through this field when supported. The installed desktop UI directly maps the server's `most_used_reasoning_effort` and `most_used_reasoning_effort_percentage` into the displayed statistic. Its English labels separately map `xhigh` to **Extra High** and `ultra` to **Ultra**; simply translating Ultra as Extra High does not explain the observed English value.

It is plausible that this statistic aggregates normalized `xhigh` requests originating from Ultra sessions, but the server-side attribution, denominator, and time window remain unverified. If this is intentional, explaining that distinction in the UI would resolve the ambiguity.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.40934 (build 20770, prod), verified through the desktop app's version/update tool on October 19, 2026.

### What subscription do you have?

Pro (200 USD)

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64.

### What issue are you seeing?

On October 19, 2026 (UTC+8), automatic approval review repeatedly failed with:

```text
Automatic approval review failed: Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.
The action was not executed because automatic approval review could not be completed.
This is a review failure, not a determination that the action is unsafe.
Do not bypass the approval check; resolve the error or ask the user for guidance.
```

This blocked a user-authorized local Windows installer build. The main agent remained able to work and successfully compiled the Release application, but could not complete the final NSIS packaging step because its request to run the packaging tool outside the sandbox failed at automatic approval review, before command execution.

The same capacity error also blocked read-only browser state inspection earlier in the session. It recurred across multiple attempts, including a later request narrowed to packaging the already-built application with existing local NSIS tools.

The error correctly says this is a review-service failure rather than an unsafe-action determination. However, it still stops the workflow. "Please try a different model" does not identify whether it means the main task model or the separate reviewer, or provide an actionable reviewer recovery control. No one-time manual approval path was surfaced to the agent in these failed tool responses.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence, rather than a deterministic way to trigger a capacity incident:

1. Run the Windows desktop app with `sandbox_mode = workspace-write` and `approvals_reviewer = auto_review`.
2. Explicitly ask the agent to build a local Tauri application's NSIS installer.
3. Request approval for the normal build command. Automatic review fails with the capacity error above before it runs.
4. Continue permitted work inside the sandbox. In this case the Release application eventually compiled successfully.
5. Attempt NSIS packaging using an existing local tool cache. Sandboxed execution of `makensis.exe` fails with Windows error 623 (Illegal System DLL Relocation).
6. Request approval to run only the final packaging step outside the sandbox. Automatic review again fails with the same capacity error; the packaging command is never executed.

The sandbox/tool-loader problem explains why escalation was needed; this report concerns the separate approval-service availability failure that prevented recovery.

### What is the expected behavior?

Keep the approval boundary intact, but provide an actionable recovery path when the reviewer service is unavailable:

- Surface service unavailability distinctly from a policy denial, including a retryable state and useful retry guidance.
- Offer a policy-permitted one-time human approval path, or another supported recovery mechanism. If managed policy forbids human approval, explain that restriction explicitly.
- Clarify which model is at capacity and whether changing the task model can actually resolve reviewer availability.
- Allow retrying the exact blocked step without repeating completed build work.

### Additional information

Related September reports:
- #45374 reports the same capacity error during browser operations.
- #45395 reports reviewer capacity errors and their effect on normal operations.

This is a new report for a verified October desktop version and a Windows build workflow. The symptom resembles those reports, but the underlying cause and whether any earlier fix applies have not been established.

The impact is a blocked authorized workflow despite successful local compilation and available local packaging tools. This report does not establish a relationship between reviewer billing policy and the capacity failure.

items.title: Windows 10 Computer Use: proven async/task deadlock cycle and reversible workaround for Sky 0.7.8

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
This report builds on [#35446](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/35446) and [#54784](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/54784). The additional evidence is an exact live operation/task/delegate/event identity proof reproduced in two fresh processes, plus an independently implemented, hash-pinned, reversible workaround for the currently affected helper. Existing diagnoses and workaround proposals are acknowledged; this is not a claim to have first discovered the threading problem.

## Summary

The native Windows capture helper synchronously waits for SoftwareBitmap conversion inside its FrameArrived callback. In two independent reproductions we verified the **exact object identity** between the operation awaited by that callback and the continuation of the blocked conversion task. The worker waits for a Direct3D critical section owned by the callback thread. The callback waits for the event that this operation's completion handler would signal. This closes the dependency cycle using live object addresses and verified code, rather than temporal correlation alone.

An independently implemented local workaround moves the original callback body to an MTA worker and makes the capture callback return promptly. Restoring the signed original reproduces the failure; restoring the workaround restores capture. The accompanying minimal ZIP contains only the patcher, helper discovery script, reconstruction delta, English instructions and checksums. Local investigation reports, diagnostic logs, source builders and test harnesses are excluded from this download. The patcher requires no compiler or Python to apply. This is not an official or generally certified binary fix.

## Environment

- Windows 10 Pro 22H2, build 19045, x64.
- Installed desktop package: `OpenAI.Codex_26.1013.4894.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0`.
- Computer Use plugin `26.1013.40934`; `@oai/sky` `0.7.8`.
- NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti; driver `32.0.16.1742`.
- Native helper original: 1,551,152 bytes; valid OpenAI Authenticode signature; SHA-256 `B6B0E4979B89E5C22DAB866F0974BC817C0D08CB359E1C2DD7BE3DCCB9E181EB`.
- The installed package version above was read from the installation; subscription details were not collected.

## Reproduction

1. Use the installed Computer Use plugin and its ordinary `@oai/sky` API in its supported JavaScript session. Open a blank Notepad window.
2. Call `list_windows()`, uniquely select the returned Notepad window, rehydrate it with `get_window()`, and activate it.
3. Call `get_window_state({window, include_screenshot:true, include_text:false})`.
4. With the original helper the call fails with `FrameArrived timed out: timed out waiting on channel`. In the two new identity-proof runs this took 2,235 ms and 2,180 ms. The callback has already received a frame; the blocked wait occurs during conversion.
5. Attach the supplied read-only diagnostic to the **native capture helper**, not Notepad or a game. Verify the expected binary hashes before applying its build-specific offsets.

All helper launches and captures used the normal Sky API. No custom helper protocol client or direct helper launch was used.

## Exact dependency proof

The collector finds live callback and worker frames and derives addresses from preserved registers. It does not hard-code the object addresses below.

| Object/thread | Reproduction A | Reproduction B, fresh process |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Callback thread | 25740 | 10196 |
| Conversion worker | 19056 | 30208 |
| Async operation O | `0x21c40ff30a0` | `0x1ff2ce030a0` |
| Conversion task T | `0x21c40fd05c0` | `0x1ff2cde05c0` |
| Continuation C | `0x21c40ff4950` | `0x1ff2ce048f0` |
| Completion delegate D | `0x21c415523b0` | `0x1ff2d2a1b60` |
| Waited event E | `0xd4c` | `0xd0c` |
| Critical section L | `0x21bbb67f680` | `0x1fee52c8080` |

Both reproductions passed all these identity checks:

```text
[initialChore+0x18] == T
[T+0x68] == C
[C+0x38] == T
[C+0x48] == O                  // exact operation awaited by callback
[[O+0x88]+0x30] == D           // retained completion delegate
[O+0x90] == helper+0x1230e0    // registered completion Invoke
[vtable(D)+0x18] == helper+0x1230e0
[D+8] == E                    // same event the callback is waiting for
L.OwningThread == callbackThreadId
```

T is still running, O is Started, and `NtQueryEvent` reports E unsignaled. The event was queried through a duplicated handle with query-only access; it was not signaled by the diagnostic. The continuation list contains C, with no next continuation in these observations.

Microsoft public PDBs matching the loaded Windows binaries identify:

- O: `MF::AsyncOperation<Windows::Graphics::Imaging::SoftwareBitmap*>`.
- T: `Concurrency::details::_Task_impl<ComPtr<ISoftwareBitmap>>`.
- C's entry: `_UnrealizedChore::_InvokeBridge<..._ContinuationTaskHandle<..., lambda_a9d737a0130ce47f4b8afa7a5b7870de,...>>`.
- Worker stack: `MediaFrameHelpers::CreateCopyWithAlphaFromSurface` → `dxrt11::Direct3DSurface::get_Description` → `NDXGI::CResource::GetDesc` → critical-section wait.

Verified RTMediaFrame instructions establish the meaning of these edges: `_InitialTaskHandle::_Init` obtains the bitmap before calling `_FinalizeAndRunContinuations`; `_RunTaskContinuations` consumes `[T+0x68]`; C's `_Continue` reads its parent T and operation O; its lambda calls `MF::AsyncOperation::NotifyCompletion`, which marks completion and calls `AsyncBaseFTM::FireCompletion`. The helper's registered `Invoke` calls `SetEvent([D+8])`.

Thus the observed cycle is:

```text
callback thread -> waits E -> requires completion of O
O -> completion continuation C -> requires task T to finish
T worker -> waits L -> owned by callback thread
```

The claim is about this concrete dependency cycle. It does not require guessing every internal Direct3D lock.

## Relevant RVAs and provenance

Helper RVAs for the original SHA above:

- `0x42489`: FrameArrived body; `0x42bae`: registers completion; `0x42c97`: synchronous wait call.
- `0x12313f`: loads `INFINITE`; `0x123144`: calls `WaitForSingleObject`; `0x123149`: return address in the blocked stack.
- `0x1230e0`: completion handler signaling its retained event.
- `0x460c4`: `ISoftwareBitmapStatics::CreateCopyFromSurfaceAsync` call, verified against the official interface binding.

`RTMediaFrame.dll` SHA-256: `fb6b491b57a063436d4d0858ac4ab537e22b8d54578ba4149a6ac026342cb43e`. PDB `RtMediaFrame.pdb`, GUID `6f2649cf-304f-e492-ba1a-b17fb8bc5e24`, age 1, obtained from Microsoft's public symbol server.

Key RTMediaFrame RVAs: `0x16134` initial-task `_Init`; `0x15fa4` finalize/run; `0x1687c` continuation-list traversal; `0x150f4` C's `_Continue`; `0x114c8` completion lambda; `0x14318` NotifyCompletion; `0x13880` FireCompletion. All offsets are version-specific.

## Independent workaround and validation

The original callback body is left intact. Two original mapped-image sites change: the screenshot-delegate allocation call at `0x3fb0a`, and its Invoke vtable pointer at `0x12dec8`. Newly compiled glue expands that delegate from 56 to 64 bytes for a once-only dispatch flag, retains its reference, starts an MTA worker and returns from the capture callback. The worker invokes the original body, balances successful RoInitialize with RoUninitialize, and releases its reference. Creation/initialization failure paths roll back ownership/dispatch state. The original allocator's alignment-only deallocator was checked separately.

The PE builder adds compiler-produced code, relocations and unwind metadata in separate sections. Structural checks verify unchanged original imports, entry point, TLS and DLL security characteristics, no RWX sections, and relocation at three alternative bases. Five new runtime-function entries were checked.

Isolated harness results: 204 stub-callback/lifetime cases, 205 workers including an injected initialization failure, 1,000 duplicate dispatches suppressed, explicit allocation/reference cleanup and thread-creation failure/retry checks, 409 explicit unwind walks, and process handle count 104 before/104 after. **These are not 204 real screenshots.** `CaptureStackBackTrace` stopped at the privately mapped test code on this Windows build; the harness reports those stops and explicitly verifies with `RtlLookupFunctionEntry`/`RtlVirtualUnwind` instead.

Real normal-API tests succeeded with Notepad (capture, click, keyboard), Paint (capture/menu), and AION2 (capture only). Sampled live counters in two helper lifetimes reported 17/17 and 13/13 completed capture jobs with no initialization/thread-creation failures. Counts are jobs, not distinct visually reviewed screenshots. The original/candidate return-and-reapply experiment reproduced the error with the original and successful capture with the candidate. After both new identity-proof runs, restoring the candidate restored a correct Notepad capture in 187 ms.

Short local latency samples with the workaround: Notepad capture 68–93 ms; AION2 1920x1080 capture 142 and 224 ms. These measure the awaited local API call, not the full model/UI interaction loop or a baseline against a working original.

## Scope and remaining engineering work

The operation/task identity gap is closed for these reproductions. The experimental workaround still needs production lifecycle review: window-close/cancel/shutdown races, unrelated conversion stalls, bounded outstanding work, error delivery, and long-duration/resource testing. The original conversion wait remains unbounded inside its worker. Tests on other Windows/GPU/build combinations are not available. A product fix should express the scheduling and resource ownership directly in maintained source, with cancellation and bounded cleanup, rather than transplanting these binary offsets.

An earlier apparently occluded-window failure was confounded by the user's Alt+Tab during the test and is not treated as a confirmed independent bug or as proof of successful occluded capture. Swift/Appshot hotkey failures were not linked to this native deadlock and are outside the claim.

## Download, apply and roll back the experimental workaround

Download: [codex-win10-capture-workaround.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33669601/codex-win10-capture-workaround.zip)


Verified attachment file: `codex-win10-capture-workaround.zip` (34,151 bytes; 5 files). SHA-256: `4EE8861317770229B7EA15DA6A685AAFEFE5CE66D97F9D858CB157F96CD5EA55`. The uploaded archive was downloaded again and verified byte-for-byte against the minimal package. The installer and delta are unchanged from the previously tested version; the supported-original and reconstructed-candidate hashes below are unchanged.

The ZIP contains exactly five files at its root: `Repair-Capture.ps1`, `Find-CaptureHelper.ps1`, `capture-fix.delta.json`, `README.md` and `SHA256SUMS.txt`. It does **not** contain the proprietary native/Swift helper, Windows DLLs/PDBs, screenshots or memory dumps. The delta reconstructs the exact validated candidate from the user's own supported original. It contains byte edits, our newly compiled scheduling code and required PE metadata, rather than redistributing the complete vendor executable.

Supported original SHA-256:

```text
B6B0E4979B89E5C22DAB866F0974BC817C0D08CB359E1C2DD7BE3DCCB9E181EB
```

Expected candidate SHA-256:

```text
4F1BF5FAD6750D712CD1DA91848FAE410CB87C407B7F791025B68D6F45C68810
```

Extract and inspect the ZIP. Run `Find-CaptureHelper.ps1` to obtain the actual running native helper's path, rather than guessing an old cache location. Set `$helperPath` to that exact discovered path. From the folder containing the five extracted files:

```powershell
# First: read-only compatibility check.
.\Repair-Capture.ps1 -Mode Check -TargetPath $helperPath

# Close the desktop app normally before applying.
.\Repair-Capture.ps1 -Mode Apply -TargetPath $helperPath

# To restore the signed original, close the app and use the same target path.
.\Repair-Capture.ps1 -Mode Rollback -TargetPath $helperPath
```

`$helperPath` must be assigned before these commands; full instructions are in `README.md`. Reopen the desktop app after Apply or Rollback and use Computer Use normally. Do not start the native helper directly. The candidate is unsigned; no security setting, execution-policy bypass or protection disablement is part of this procedure.

Apply verifies the original's pinned hash and valid signature, reconstructs the candidate and verifies its pinned hash, preserves a verified original backup, stops only helpers using the exact specified file, and replaces it atomically. Rollback requires that backup and restores the original hash/signature. Unknown hashes, an altered delta, an unrelated existing backup and an updated/replaced target are refused. An app update may replace the helper; never remove the version checks to force a new binary.

The portable installer passed ten checks on disposable files under **Windows PowerShell 5.1.19041.7802 and PowerShell 7.6.5**: read-only Check, exact candidate reconstruction with signed backup, repeated Apply, signed-original restoration/repeated Rollback, unknown target refusal, missing-backup refusal, unrelated-backup preservation, corrupted-delta refusal, preservation of a target changed after Apply, and staging cleanup. The same installer was then exercised on the live installation: Apply returned a correct normal-API Notepad capture in 190 ms; Rollback restored the original hash and valid signature; reapplying restored a correct capture in 179 ms. The desktop app remained open during this local check. A full desktop-app restart and Windows reboot have not been tested. The candidate is left active.

This workaround targets the supported helper hash only. Matching the app version or error message alone is insufficient. Other Windows/GPU combinations, every lifecycle race and long-term stability remain unvalidated. Please provide a maintained, signed official fix with appropriate object ownership, cancellation and bounded cleanup.

items.title: Codex Cloud: recent workspace changes unavailable on task continuation while older contents remain

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: codex-web
labels.description: Issues related to Codex Web

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

During continuation of an ongoing Codex Cloud development conversation, recent workspace changes were no longer available while older contents remained. This interrupted the work.

- Product: Codex Cloud, using an OpenAI-managed cloud task environment.
- Observed: October 19, 2026 (UTC).
- Exact frontend/backend versions were not captured.

The accessible workspace appears to present an earlier working state. This is an observation, not an established explanation: the exact task-to-filesystem mapping and any backend lifecycle transition still require verification by Support. Permanent physical deletion, rollback, replacement, or a shared cause with other reports have not been established.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deterministic reproducer is available. The reported sequence was:

1. Work in an ongoing Codex Cloud development conversation.
2. Continue that conversation and inspect its associated cloud workspace.
3. Find recent working contents unavailable while older files remain.

Please correlate the original task and its preceding storage/snapshots through the existing private support conversation.

### What is the expected behavior?

Continuing the original task should retain its working files within the supported persistence window. If a task cannot recover its prior working state, the product should clearly disclose that condition, identify the applicable recovery window, and provide a supported preservation/recovery path.

Please investigate:

- Whether continuation presented an older or different filesystem state.
- Whether the preceding workspace and snapshots can be preserved and restored before cleanup.
- What persistence guarantees, transition warnings, and automatic checkpoint/export mechanisms apply.

The official guide directs users with unavailable task files to Support and describes a default saved-VM recovery window of up to seven days:
https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001545-using-codex-cloud

### Additional information

Official private support has confirmed escalation to a support specialist. Correlation details are being handled privately; this public report includes no account email, task/environment identifiers, private project details, source code, or raw transcripts.

Related symptoms: #52765 and #53902. Those reports concern Dots cloud computers. This issue concerns Codex Cloud and is filed separately to make the affected product clear; a common backend cause is not established. An earlier generic corroborating comment was posted on #52765 before that product distinction was checked.

Submitted by the assistant at the affected user's explicit request to report the incident to official support and GitHub.

items.title: [Windows app] Side-chat messages lack the Edit action available in the main conversation

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Exact application version has not been collected. This report concerns the Codex interface in the current ChatGPT desktop application on Windows (formerly the standalone Codex desktop app), not the CLI or IDE extension.

### What subscription do you have?

Not provided.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11, 64-bit (x64). The application UI is in Simplified Chinese.

### What issue are you seeing?

The message-editing affordance is inconsistent between a normal/main conversation and a side conversation in the same desktop application window.

- **Main conversation, in the left/main pane:** below a previously sent user message, at the lower-right edge of the message, there is a Copy icon and a small pencil/Edit icon. The reporter can use the pencil to edit an earlier message.
- **Side conversation, in the right-hand pane:** below the reporter's own previously sent message, the corresponding footer shows the timestamp and a Copy icon, but **no pencil/Edit icon**. The reporter therefore has no equivalent visible way to edit that side-chat message.
- Both panes can be inspected side by side in the same application window, making the difference directly visible. This was observed with the side chat's assistant response already present, rather than merely while entering an unsent prompt.

This is a **missing Edit entry point / UI consistency issue**, not an error after clicking Send in an editor. No "Failed to edit message" error is being reported in this case, because the side chat does not expose the edit control in the first place.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open the Windows desktop application and enter the Codex view.
2. Open a normal/main conversation that contains a previously sent user message.
3. Inspect that user message's lower-right footer/message actions (hover over it if necessary). Observe the Copy and pencil/Edit controls.
4. Open a side conversation in the right-hand pane of the same window.
5. Send a user message in the side conversation and let the assistant respond.
6. Inspect the side conversation's own sent user message in the same way.
7. Compare the message actions: the main conversation offers Edit, but the side conversation shows Copy without an equivalent Edit control.

These steps describe the reporter's observed UI; no claim is made about a code-level root cause.

### What is the expected behavior?

User-authored messages in a side conversation should offer the same discoverable Edit action and edit/resubmit workflow as user-authored messages in the main conversation.

This expectation applies to messages actually sent in the side conversation, **not** to inherited/read-only parent-conversation context. Editing a side-chat message should not modify the parent conversation.

If editing is intentionally unsupported for side conversations, please make that limitation explicit in the UI/documentation and clarify the intended difference rather than silently omitting the action.

### Additional information

- **Observed/reported:** October 19, 2026, approximately 12:29, Asia/Shanghai (UTC+08:00).
- **Scope:** Windows desktop UI; main chat versus right-hand side chat in the same window.
- **User impact:** the reporter can correct an earlier main-chat prompt using the existing editing workflow, but cannot find the corresponding operation for their own side-chat prompt.
- The reporter supplied a close-up of the main message footer, a close-up of the side-chat message footer, and a full-window comparison. At the reporter's request, this issue uses the textual description above **without uploading those screenshots**.
- Potentially related, but different manifestations:
  - #25961 and #26514 describe a side-chat Edit control that exists but fails when submitting the edit.
  - #48567 concerns previous-prompt editing in CLI/TUI side chats. This report is specifically about the missing desktop UI affordance.

items.title: Remote-control managed daemon fails to create control socket in Debian PRoot on Android

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Environment

- Device: Android phone (Samsung Galaxy F15 5G)
- Host environment: Termux running Debian 13 (trixie) arm64 via PRoot
- Codex CLI installed through npm
- CLI version reported by `codex --version`: `codex-cli 0.162.1`
- Managed app-server version after running `codex app-server daemon update`: `0.163.0`

## Problem

The managed app-server daemon cannot start with remote control enabled. Startup repeatedly fails because the control socket is missing, while the daemon stderr reports `Error: File exists (os error 17)`.

Representative output from `codex remote-control start`:

```text
Starting app-server daemon with remote control enabled...
Error: app server did not become ready on /root/.codex/app-server-control/app-server-control.sock

Daemon used app-server:
  path: /root/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/current/bin/codex
  version: 0.163.0

Managed app-server stderr:
  Error: File exists (os error 17)
Caused by:
    0: failed to connect to /root/.codex/app-server-control/app-server-control.sock
    1: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install Codex CLI in Debian 13 arm64 running inside Termux/PRoot on Android.
2. Run `codex app-server daemon enable-remote-control`.
3. Run `codex remote-control start` (also reproduced with `codex app-server daemon restart`).
4. Observe that the daemon does not become ready at `~/.codex/app-server-control/app-server-control.sock`.
5. Run `codex remote-control pair`; it fails to connect to the same missing socket.

## Observed behavior

- `codex app-server daemon stop` reports `{"status":"notRunning", ...}`.
- `ps -ef | grep '[c]odex'` shows no Codex process after the failed start.
- The PID file remained at `~/.codex/app-server-daemon/daemon.pid` and referenced PID 7615, but no corresponding process was visible.
- Initially, `ls -lai ~/.codex/app-server-control/` showed an inaccessible entry displayed as `l??????????` for `app-server-control.sock`, while `stat` reported no such file. Renaming the control directory and creating a fresh one did not fix the startup failure.
- Updating the managed app-server changed its version from `0.162.1` to `0.163.0`, but the same error remained.
- **Workaround / contrast:** `codex remote-control --no-daemon` succeeds and prints:
  `This machine is available for remote control as localhost.`
  However, `codex remote-control pair` in a second session still fails because it expects the missing managed-daemon control socket.

## Expected behavior

The managed daemon should start and create a usable control socket in this environment, or report a clear unsupported-environment error with a documented workaround. The foreground mode working while managed-daemon startup fails suggests the issue is specific to the managed daemon startup path or its interaction with PRoot.

## Additional context

I did not grant host root access; commands are running as root inside the Debian PRoot environment. Reinstalling/updating the npm CLI and updating the managed app-server did not resolve the issue.
