items.title: Enforce a shared spending budget before model requests across root and subagents

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: rate-limits
labels.description: Issues related to rate limits, quotas, and token usage reporting

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex desktop on macOS, app `26.1013.40934` (build `20770`), bundled runtime `0.163.0-alpha.10.2`.

Source references below use commit [`4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4), the commit targeted by release tag `rust-v0.163.0-alpha.10.2`. The referenced files were compared with that commit. The shared-budget implementation was also checked on `main` at `89461ea6833832b0551ce24ee32205824d5c108d` and is unchanged.

### What feature would you like to see?

Extend the existing shared rollout budget so it reserves capacity **before each model request**, accounts for all priced usage, and prevents further automatic model work after exhaustion across the root and its descendants.

**User story:** As a desktop user authorizing a long-running task, I want one enforceable spending limit for the whole task so that subagents, follow-ups, retries and compaction cannot continue consuming my allowance beyond that authorization.

This is a focused implementation companion to the incident report at https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/55168. It supplies a runtime contract for the broader budget request at https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/45536; estimates, model comparisons and a new usage dashboard are outside this issue.

#### Observed behavior and existing ownership

The incident's fixed 36-hour response ledger recorded **8,949,499,238 input-plus-output tokens across 50,465 unique responses**, including **8,788,141,824 cached input tokens**. These are processed tokens, not unique text, full-price uncached tokens or a verified invoice. The inspected large goals had no configured token budget, so this does not demonstrate violation of an explicit budget. A concurrency cap alone cannot bound repeated work over time.

The runtime already has the appropriate ownership boundary:

- [`LocalAgentRuntime` shares one `Arc<RolloutBudget>` across the root and cloned subagent controls](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/runtime.rs#L182-L204).
- [`RolloutBudget::record_usage`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/rollout_budget.rs#L47-L66) accounts reported usage and then checks exhaustion. With no configuration it returns `false`. The fallback counts weighted output and uncached input; server-provided `codex_rollout_budget_units` take precedence when present.
- [Completed usage is passed to budget accounting](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/session/mod.rs#L5088-L5101), and [exhaustion returns `SessionBudgetExceeded`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/budget.rs#L11-L16). Post-response accounting alone cannot reserve the remaining allowance against concurrent requests.
- [Goal continuation can start another idle turn](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/ext/goal/src/runtime.rs#L436-L502). The spending decision needs to apply to model requests within turns as well as new turns: one incident coordinator produced 1,860 responses in only two turns.
- [Goal token accounting excludes cached input](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/ext/goal/src/accounting.rs#L570-L575). This is intentional behavior and must not silently become a proxy for billed credits.

#### Bounded technical specification

1. **One shared admission decision per request.** Extend the existing budget owner with atomic reservation and settlement. Before dispatch, require `settled usage + outstanding reservations + requested reservation <= authorized limit`. Apply this to ordinary sampling, foreground/background compaction, and every retry that may incur additional provider work. Do not create a separate budget for each child or replenish the budget on follow-up.
2. **Honest units and bounds.** Include cached input, uncached input, output and any other priced request component. Use authoritative provider units/rates and bounded request parameters when available. A strict spending guarantee requires a conservative pre-request upper bound or provider-enforced cap. If that contract is unavailable, expose the limit as an estimate or weighted-token limit, not a guaranteed USD/credit ceiling. Do not charge cached input at the uncached rate merely to simplify the counter.
3. **Conservative recovery.** Settle each reported response once. Preserve unresolved reservations when a dispatched request times out, is cancelled, or returns no usage; missing usage is not evidence of zero cost. A retry may perform additional billable work even when local settlement is idempotent. Reconcile uncertainty before reopening capacity, and preserve budget identity, settled usage, pending reservations and exhaustion across resume/restart using existing persistence boundaries.
4. **Exhaustion closes model admission.** Return a typed budget-exhausted result without another provider call. Follow-ups, nested workers and automatic goal continuations must honor the same state. Preserve completed work and stop scheduling new model requests; do not indiscriminately kill unrelated shell/MCP operations. Requests already dispatched may still incur charges. Increasing the limit must be an explicit user action, not a model decision.
5. **Explicit authorization for unattended work.** Use the existing configuration/protocol surface to distinguish a finite limit from explicitly authorized unbounded operation. Missing configuration must not be presented as spending protection. Report settled, reserved and remaining units plus the stop reason without requiring a new dashboard.

Proposed change locations, reusing existing packages:

```text
codex-rs/core/src/rollout_budget.rs             reservation and settlement
codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/               shared admission and exhaustion
codex-rs/core/src/session/                     sampling dispatch and usage hooks
codex-rs/core/src/compact_remote_v2*.rs         compaction coverage
codex-rs/ext/goal/src/                         continuation respects exhaustion
codex-rs/state/                               durable budget state and recovery
```

These are proposed ownership locations, not a request for a new generic scheduler or accounting framework.

#### Acceptance criteria

- Three concurrent workers contend for the last request allowance: only requests with an atomic reservation reach the fake provider, and total reservations plus settled usage remain within the configured bound.
- A single turn containing many sampling/tool cycles cannot bypass admission; nested children, resumed workers and goal continuations use the same budget.
- Cached-heavy requests and foreground/background compaction consume the correct defined units. Goal-token totals and spending units remain separately labeled.
- Duplicate completion delivery settles once; a retry that performs new provider work receives its own reservation. Missing usage, disconnect and cancellation retain conservative accounting.
- Restart/resume neither resets an exhausted budget nor frees unresolved reservations. A crash between reservation and dispatch has a conservative, documented recovery path.
- Exhaustion emits a typed result, preserves completed output, and produces no further unreserved model requests. Only an explicit limit increase permits additional spending.
- Verify these scenarios with deterministic local/fake-provider tests; reproducing the 36-hour incident on a paid account is unnecessary.

#### Dependencies and exclusions

The billing-unit definition and a bounded per-request cost contract are prerequisites for claiming a strict monetary ceiling. The existing `codex_rollout_budget_units` field is an integration point; its presence alone does not establish that it equals credits or USD.

Related investigations, not asserted blockers or parent/child issues:

- Incident evidence: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/55168
- Broader task-budget product request: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/45536
- Missing response usage: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/37138
- Provider quota exhaustion admission, a separate resource condition: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/39582

Excluded: proving incorrect billing or obtaining refunds, repairing the separate concurrency-admission race, changing model defaults, redesigning context compaction, adding a semantic progress watchdog, and estimating task cost or comparing models. Those concerns can be investigated independently of this shared request-budget contract.

### Additional information

This is a proposed safeguard supported by source inspection, not an implemented patch or proof that one defect caused the entire incident. The linked incident has sanitized evidence and offline accounting reproductions available; this issue contains no raw prompts, credentials or private project contents.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### Environment
- Windows desktop app, local PowerShell workspace; observed on 2026-10-19 (Asia/Shanghai).
- App update checker reports installedVersion `26.1007.71326`, build `20398`, channel `prod`.
- Installed Windows package version: `26.1007.9446.0` (a separate component version).
- Bundled executor: `codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.17.2`.
- Effective task instructions: `approval_policy=never`, `sandbox_mode=danger-full-access`. These are not asserted to override another policy.
- Subscription not collected.

### Observed issue
A user-authorized, narrowly scoped local application update was rejected before execution with an opaque error containing:
```text
exec_command failed: CreateProcess
Rejected(... blocked by policy)
```
The intended command would use the application's normal loopback shutdown endpoint, verify process exit, copy an explicit manifest of four UI source files and their associated static build assets after hash/backup checks, and start the local application normally. It did not request business-data mutations, credential access, cloud deployment, or deletion. No force-kill was proposed.

This is an observed failure, not a newly run minimal reproduction. The command was not executed, and the blocked outcome has not been pursued through another transport. The exact enforcing component, decision ID and detailed rationale remain unknown.

Two earlier shutdown requests were separately rejected by the application for missing normal source headers; these did not stop the application. The later command included the source headers required by the application's existing shutdown implementation, but was rejected by the execution tool before it ran. We cannot establish that these distinct failures share a cause.

### Approval / recovery gap
The user explicitly authorized the local update. In the desktop composer, entering `/approve` did not expose an actionable denial picker. Read-only inspection shows that the installed client contains an approval command conditioned on eligible denial records, but does not prove this particular rejection created one.

The current official Auto-review documentation says `approval_policy=never` does not generate interactive review requests. Therefore this report does **not** attribute the rejection to Auto-review, and does not assume `/approve` must resolve it.

The user restarted the desktop app; the update checker still reported the same version and `restart_required`. We cannot establish whether that status is stale or whether a pending update did not apply.

### Expected behavior / questions
Please identify the supported diagnostic and recovery path:
1. Which privacy-safe fields identify the enforcing policy for a pre-execution `blocked by policy` rejection with no reason or actionable denial?
2. If eligible for narrow manual approval, how should this Windows version expose the record? If ineligible, what supported escalation/support path applies?
3. Is a persistent `restart_required` after restart a known update-reporting issue?

Please preserve security restrictions; we are not requesting a bypass or a global policy relaxation.

Related reports: #50524 and #54746 have similar symptoms; a shared root cause is unconfirmed.

### Privacy / scope
No credentials, private paths, source code, business data, full session transcript or raw logs are attached. The local app's update remains unloaded.

### Additional non-executing source inspection

The published source tag matching the reported executor version, [rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2 / windows_dangerous_commands.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2/codex-rs/shell-command/src/command_safety/windows_dangerous_commands.rs), contains a best-effort PowerShell token classifier that can return dangerous when a URL and a Start-Process/Invoke-Item token coexist in the parsed invocation. The source comments explicitly describe best-effort token scanning rather than a full PowerShell parser.

Our retained operation description includes a loopback health/shutdown request and ordinary process startup in the same command. This makes the published classifier a diagnostic lead, **not confirmed attribution**: we have no evaluator trace, normalized argument vector, matching-rule receipt, or proof that this exact source implementation produced our rejection. We have not executed or rewritten the denied action to test the hypothesis, and have not changed permission settings.

Could a maintainer identify the actual enforcing evaluator and its privacy-safe decision trace for this rejection, and clarify the supported review or fixed-version route if the classifier applies? Please distinguish a confirmed restriction from a command-classification defect. We are not asking for a workaround or a global relaxation.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Installed macOS app metadata: version `26.1013.40934`, build `20770`, bundle ID `com.openai.codex` (displayed as ChatGPT). These values were read from the installed app’s Info.plist; the About dialog was not inspected.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Apple Silicon. `uname -mprs`: `Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm`.

### What issue are you seeing?

The built-in browser opens and renders a local development website normally for the user, but the agent cannot discover or control browser tabs. The supplied `mcp__cua_repl.js` tool is present and executes, but browser access repeatedly fails with:

```text
The browser access host is unavailable
```

Calling `await cua.getState();` successfully discovers native applications, while the browser portion returns:

```json
{
  "browsers": [],
  "errors": ["Browsers: Error: The browser access host is unavailable"]
}
```

This prevents the agent from inspecting the rendered local app even though its in-app browser tab is visibly open and working.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed repeatedly in an existing local project chat on October 18, 2026:

1. Open a working local development page in the built-in browser (observed at `http://localhost:3112/`).
2. Ask the agent to inspect that tab.
3. Call `await cua.getState();` through `mcp__cua_repl.js`: native apps are discovered, but browser inventory fails as shown above.
4. Directly request the existing tab:

```js
await cua.getTab({ url: "http://localhost:3112/" }, { browser: "iab" });
```

This returns the same host-unavailable error.
5. Explicitly select `@Browser` in the user message and retry: same result.
6. Reset the tool’s JavaScript session with `mcp__cua_repl.js_reset`, then retry direct tab acquisition: same result.

Feedback ID: `01a1485d-d37b-7a41-8625-eb9eeced1667`

The user successfully submitted in-app feedback before requesting this GitHub report.

### What is the expected behavior?

The agent should be able to discover and inspect an enabled, open built-in browser tab. If the browser access host cannot initialize or connect, the app should provide an actionable diagnostic or supported recovery procedure.

### Additional information

- Repeated retries, an explicit Browser mention, and a tool-session reset did not resolve the issue.
- A full desktop-app restart and a fresh standalone chat have not yet been confirmed as tested.
- No app settings, browser profiles, security controls, or plugin files were changed during these checks.
- Root cause is unknown. This report does not claim the local website, account permissions, or a particular update caused it.
- Related macOS report: #24335. That report describes missing browser tools; here the CUA tool is available and native discovery works, but the browser host fails explicitly.
- Related browser-discovery report on Windows: #54968. Same root cause is not established.

Please advise on a supported recovery procedure that preserves existing chats and browser data.

items.body:
### What is the type of issue?

Documentation is missing.

### What is the issue?

We need to verify the role, UTF-8 hash/length and occurrence count of our own developer payload in an actual stock Windows Desktop request. We are not asking for private platform instructions, credentials, or unrelated conversations.

At public source commit `74e804deeb1241d5fe699b31fb319f7d46454c42`, rollout-trace records request payloads and inference/thread/turn IDs. The root startup method in `codex-rs/rollout-trace/src/thread.rs` reads `CODEX_ROLLOUT_TRACE_ROOT` from the process environment; we have not established a supported Desktop control that limits collection before recording to one selected thread/turn.

Is there a supported stock Windows Desktop operation for this, and which shipped builds provide it? A local verifier limited to our supplied payload would also work if it derives its result from the actual assembled request and reports coverage limits.

For WebSocket continuation, what supported evidence distinguishes the full logical input from the transmitted delta and links `previous_response_id`, especially after an untraced warmup? We have not enabled rollout tracing in this read-only check and have not established that the currently installed Desktop engine matches that public commit.

If this is not supported, please confirm that limitation or the appropriate Desktop support channel. Our accepted Desktop result in this validation stage is one successful `UserPromptSubmit` target-blocking probe; it does not establish request content.

This is a capability/documentation question, not a claim of a confirmed Desktop request-assembly bug. No raw requests, private configuration, session identifiers, credentials, or trace bundles are attached.

### Where did you find it?

Version-pinned public source inspected:
- [rollout-trace README](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/74e804deeb1241d5fe699b31fb319f7d46454c42/codex-rs/rollout-trace/README.md)
- [Root startup and trace context](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/74e804deeb1241d5fe699b31fb319f7d46454c42/codex-rs/rollout-trace/src/thread.rs)
- [Inference request recording](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/74e804deeb1241d5fe699b31fb319f7d46454c42/codex-rs/rollout-trace/src/inference.rs)
- [HTTP / WebSocket request assembly](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/74e804deeb1241d5fe699b31fb319f7d46454c42/codex-rs/core/src/client.rs)

Related documented surfaces:
- [Advanced configuration / observability](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-advanced#observability-and-telemetry)
- [App Server / stored thread reads](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server#read-a-stored-thread-without-resuming)

Related but distinct requests:
- #43078 asks for metadata-only reasoning-effort correlation. This question concerns our own developer content and a selected stock Desktop turn.
- #25914 asks for active Desktop thread discovery/attachment. Attaching to live conversation events alone would not establish the assembled model request.
- #35706 proposes a fuller CLI prompt-debug snapshot. A separately constructed CLI prompt is not the Desktop request under test.

We would welcome an existing supported workflow or a clear statement of the current limitation.

Five recorded failures span 8 minutes 28.282 seconds on 2026-10-19:

| UTC timestamp | Asia/Shanghai (UTC+08:00) | Selected value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 02:57:04.528Z | 10:57:04.528 | <custom-bot-id> |
| 02:57:09.113Z | 10:57:09.113 | <custom-bot-id> |
| 03:01:54.984Z | 11:01:54.984 | codex |
| 03:03:57.138Z | 11:03:57.138 | hoots |
| 03:05:32.810Z | 11:05:32.810 | <custom-bot-id> |

Each entry is `[electron-message-handler] sa_server_request_failed`, with method PATCH, routePattern `/settings/account_user_setting`, and status 409.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence on the affected account:

1. Create a custom bot using the Pets plugin. Creation succeeds and the bot remains present in the collection.
2. Select it in desktop pet settings.
3. The app displays `unable to update bot`.
4. Try built-in Codex and Hoots. Their requests receive the same 409 response.
5. Try the custom bot again several minutes later; the same conflict remains.

This is an observed sequence on one account, not a confirmed clean-account reproduction. Creation preceding the failure does not establish that creation caused it.

### What is the expected behavior?

The selected bot becomes active. If another update legitimately blocks selection, that operation should finish or expire so a subsequent selection can succeed. The UI should expose an actionable pending-update status instead of only a generic error.

### Additional information

- Confirmed direct failure: the selection endpoint rejects the request as an in-progress-update conflict. This affects both custom and built-in bots.
- A stale update/lock is a possibility, but a long-running operation or repeated concurrent updates cannot be distinguished from client logs. No backend root cause has been verified.
- Earlier in troubleshooting, the Pets plugin's `select_pet` returned the custom bot ID as `active_pet_id` successfully, while the user still reported desktop failure. Later `list_pets` readbacks returned `active_pet_id=codex`, with the custom bot still listed and inactive. No immediate independent readback was captured after the successful selection response, so this does not prove rollback. Please compare the desktop `accessory_id` path and Pets selection persistence/scoping.
- Please inspect the pending operation owner/scope, start/completion/failure state, and lock release/expiry around **2026-10-19T02:57:04Z–03:05:33Z**.
- This differs from #45397: the confirmed failure here is HTTP 409 while saving bot selection, rather than a visible overlay ignoring mouse input.
- A verified full app restart, web/cross-device comparison, and clean-account reproduction were not tested in this diagnostic pass.
- No app files, caches, or bot assets were manually modified; no bot was deleted or recreated as troubleshooting.
- Exact-error issue search found no matching report before submission.

Custom bot names/IDs, account/workspace IDs, authentication values, signed URLs, and full logs have been omitted.

items.body:
### What is the type of issue?

Documentation is missing or unclear: Windows Computer Use input completion and supported diagnostics.

### What is the issue?

Please clarify the public contract of the bundled `@oai/sky` API used through the official Node REPL on Windows. This is a documentation/support-routing question based on saved observations, not an established product defect or a complete reproduction report.

1. What does normal completion of `click` and `press_key` guarantee: target resolution, event submission, OS acceptance, or application processing?
2. Which documented, non-sensitive diagnostic fields distinguish those stages? Is the actual input executor identity or event submission result available through a supported interface?
3. Are there documented VMware Workstation input-capture or synthetic-input compatibility constraints? If investigation is appropriate, which exact version fields and minimum observations are needed, and which support channel should receive them?

Context from two separately authorized, already-ended attempts against an existing VMware Workstation window:

- A fresh accessibility tree identified the host VM menu. One index-based `sky.click` returned normally, but subsequent observations did not establish that the menu opened. A transient or unlisted menu is not excluded.
- On another occasion, the current window explicitly showed the Ctrl+Alt return-to-host hint. One `sky.press_key({window: currentWindow, key: 'Control_L+Alt_L'})` returned normally. The subsequent observation still showed that hint, so host input readiness was not established. We stopped without menu input or cleanup keys. Partial guest modifier events and final modifier state remain unknown.

An earlier index-click exception had no retained detail. A planned coordinate attempt ended before any click; it is not evidence of coordinate-click failure. These observations do not establish a common cause, a general Windows input failure, or an SDK exception in the two normally returned attempts.

The bundled Computer Use documentation was version `26.1013.31256`. This is **not** a verified Codex App, SDK/helper, Windows or VMware runtime version; those exact versions have not been collected for this question. The overview names SendInput, UI Automation and Windows.Graphics.Capture, without giving a per-call native-event or application-processing receipt.

Related user report: [#54131](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/54131) also describes a normal return without a confirmed target action in a different application. It does not establish the same cause or answer the contract questions above.

### Where did you find it?

Bundled Computer Use skill and documented `@oai/sky` API, accessed through the official Node REPL. The [official troubleshooting page](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting) and [open-source guidance](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/open-source) direct Codex reports to this repository. Please redirect this question if another maintained channel owns the bundled API contract.

No screenshot, accessibility dump, guest terminal, VM configuration, GuestInfo value, account/session identifier, credential or log attachment is included. We are requesting supported documentation, not private helper protocols, an alternate injection backend, elevation or blind retries. No new reproduction attempt is implied.

items.body:
## Summary
In the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS, a local Sites update is blocked when write_stdin attempts to send input to a running process. The permissions menu shows “Ask for approval” selected, but the tool reports that sandbox approval is disabled. No approval prompt appears.

## Environment
- ChatGPT desktop version verified during troubleshooting: 26.1007.30912 (build 20156)
- Bundle identifier: com.openai.codex
- Local execution on a personally owned Mac; personal account
- This has not been reproduced in the standalone Codex CLI.

## Steps observed
1. Select “Ask for approval” in the desktop chat.
2. Start the Sites site-workflow.mjs helper to update an existing site.
3. The process starts and waits for JSON input on stdin.
4. Invoke write_stdin to provide the input.

## Actual result
The tool rejects the call before input is delivered:

`write_stdin rejected: approval required by policy, but AskForApproval::Granular.sandbox_approval is false`

## Expected result
The desktop permission selection and effective tool policy should be consistent, with an actionable approval prompt when approval is required.

## Troubleshooting already completed
- Fully quitting and reopening the desktop app did not resolve the failure.
- The project is marked trusted.
- The user config contains no approval_policy or sandbox_approval setting.
- No project .codex/config.toml, /etc/codex/config.toml, /etc/codex/requirements.toml, or user *.config.toml profile files were found.
- Failures were observed on October 13–14, 2026; the previous successful publication was October 6.
- Only this existing site update has been tested; impact on other projects is unknown.
- Desktop diagnostics were submitted privately through Feedback. OpenAI's support assistant directed us to this repository.

No credentials, full logs, local user paths, or private diagnostic identifiers are included here. Please confirm whether this desktop integration issue belongs in this repository and advise the appropriate next diagnostic step.

items.body:
> **Source-audit correction:** The original 8,861,733,667 figure below is the legacy running-counter subtotal. Summing the more complete per-response ledger over the same fixed 36-hour window gives **8,949,499,238 tokens across 50,465 unique response IDs**, with zero duplicate response IDs and zero cross-session attribution mismatches. The difference is 87,765,571 tokens, including 260 installed compaction requests totaling 87,636,109 tokens. See the source findings appended below. The original measurement is retained for auditability.

# Excessive cached context processing in Codex desktop across 36 hours

## Summary

During 36 hours of local Codex desktop use, telemetry recorded 8,861,733,667 input-plus-output tokens across 50,204 usage increments and 293 sessions, including subagents. Of the input, 98.40% was cached. Long-running research and implementation chats generated thousands of coordination steps, repeatedly processing large contexts.

Please investigate whether this volume is expected, whether context management and agent orchestration are producing avoidable work, and whether the associated subscription and credit deductions were correct. Local telemetry establishes the volume; it does not establish the server-side charging formula or prove incorrect billing.

This appears closely related to [openai/codex#44884](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/44884). This report is additional evidence for that investigation, rather than a claim of a separate root cause.

## Environment and window

- macOS 26.6.2, Darwin 25.6.0
- Local Codex desktop sessions; runtime versions recorded in session metadata: `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`, `0.155.0-alpha.16.3`, `0.162.0-alpha.17.2` and `0.163.0-alpha.10.2` (session metadata may predate execution in this window)
- Two account identities appear in local session creation metadata; account identities are excluded from attachments
- Telemetry contains subscription plan identifiers `pro` and `promax`
- October 17, 2026 07:34:16 through October 18, 2026 19:34:16 America/Los_Angeles
- October 17, 2026 14:34:16 through October 19, 2026 02:34:16 UTC
- Main models include GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, with varying reasoning settings
- During the incident, the configured concurrent subagent limit was 40 per session

The desktop application marketing version has not been verified. Runtime version and application version should not be conflated.

## Measured usage

| Metric | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Sessions with usage in the window | 293 |
| Positive cumulative usage increments | 50,204 |
| Input tokens | 8,844,202,627 |
| Cached input tokens, included in input | 8,702,544,000 |
| Uncached input tokens | 141,658,627 |
| Output tokens | 17,531,040 |
| Reasoning output tokens, included in output | 4,458,627 |
| Total input plus output | 8,861,733,667 |

Cached input is not added to input a second time. Reasoning output is not added to output a second time. These totals represent accounted token processing, not unique text, network bytes or full-price tokens.

The three largest root workloads, including their descendants, accounted for approximately 5.602 billion, 1.470 billion and 1.349 billion tokens. The largest workload contained 152 sessions over the full 36-hour window. The full anonymous workload totals are in the prepared evidence package.

## Observed behavior

In the narrower 24-hour window inspected within this period:

- One research workload had 122 sessions including the root, 4,282 inter-agent send-message calls and 752 follow-up-task calls
- One coordinator made 1,859 positive usage increments, averaging approximately 203,000 input tokens per increment
- A separate implementation workload had only four sessions, but made 6,174 positive usage increments, with 1,027 inter-agent messages and 394 follow-up-task calls
- Two workers in that implementation workload averaged approximately 210,000 and 220,000 input tokens per increment
- Some subagent trees reached depth four
- Half-hourly scheduled continuations kept two workloads active; later continuation attempts encountered usage-limit errors

These observations show that concurrency alone does not explain the volume. Repeated steps in a small number of long-lived contexts can also produce very high usage.

Local snapshots recorded multiple allowance windows reaching 100%, and credit balances declining to zero. Account switching or resets may explain changes between windows. We cannot attribute every deduction to an account from session creator metadata, and are not claiming duplicate billing across accounts.

## Workload pattern for reproduction

This is an observed workload pattern, not a verified minimal reproduction:

1. Start a long-running research or implementation chat with tools and subagents enabled
2. Continue work through many tool operations, agent messages and follow-up tasks
3. Let the same chats continue for hours, including scheduled continuations
4. Inspect cumulative token usage increments and per-step input size
5. Compare the accounted volume and server-side quota deductions

Please avoid reproducing this at full scale on a paid account. A bounded internal replay or instrumented test should be enough to investigate the behavior.

## Expected behavior and investigation requests

Long-running tasks should avoid carrying unnecessary context through thousands of small operations. Coordination and waiting should consume as little model work as possible, and unusually expensive loops should be visible to the user before an allowance is exhausted.

Please investigate:

- Whether each recorded usage increment corresponds to a distinct billed inference
- Whether cumulative usage counters include retries, repeated accounting or child usage already counted elsewhere
- How cached input and reasoning output were weighted against the subscription allowance and purchased credits
- Whether compaction, retention of tool results or repeated agent coordination caused unnecessary context processing
- Whether the subagent limit of 40 was enforced across each complete descendant tree
- Whether guardrails can bound coordination loops and alert users to rapidly increasing usage

The recorded data does not prove a concurrency-limit breach: total sessions over time can legitimately exceed the concurrent limit.

## Evidence method and privacy

The evidence was generated from local rollout JSONL files referenced by the local thread index. For each session, the extractor walks cumulative counters in file order, including records before the window to establish the baseline. It sums positive changes within the fixed window and excludes repeated unchanged snapshots. Sessions are aggregated once each, including archived sessions indexed locally.

The extraction found zero counter decreases and zero input-plus-output arithmetic mismatches. `summary.json` records these checks. Run `python3 verify_evidence.py` to independently verify the evidence totals. `sanitized-token-events.jsonl.gz` contains timestamped positive increments, anonymous session and workload labels, model and reasoning settings, context sizes and selected rate-limit metadata. `sanitized-session-summary.csv` records anonymous parent-child relationships and per-session totals.

No prompts, responses, tool arguments or outputs, source code, original session identifiers, account identifiers, emails, usernames, workspace names, filesystem paths, credentials or authentication material are included in the sanitized telemetry files. Exact event timestamps remain for investigation. Unrecorded or unindexed activity on other devices is outside this dataset.

## Mitigation already applied

After this measurement window, concurrency was reduced to three subagents per session, with GPT-6.1 Sol and low reasoning as subagent defaults. This is a precaution, not a demonstrated fix. The main-chat default and existing schedules were unchanged by that configuration edit.


## Sanitized log sample

Each line is a positive per-session cumulative counter delta, not a raw cumulative total. Session and workload labels are anonymous.

```jsonl
{"timestamp_utc":"2026-10-17T15:45:57.414Z","session":"session-016","workload":"workload-06","model":"gpt-6-astra","reasoning_effort":"ultra","usage_delta":{"input_tokens":204944,"cached_input_tokens":197760,"cache_write_input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":467,"reasoning_output_tokens":261,"total_tokens":205411},"last_input_tokens":204944,"context_window":258400,"weekly_used_percent":91.0,"window_minutes":10080,"plan_type":"pro"}
{"timestamp_utc":"2026-10-17T15:46:04.998Z","session":"session-016","workload":"workload-06","model":"gpt-6-astra","reasoning_effort":"ultra","usage_delta":{"input_tokens":205423,"cached_input_tokens":204800,"cache_write_input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":478,"reasoning_output_tokens":139,"total_tokens":205901},"last_input_tokens":205423,"context_window":258400,"weekly_used_percent":91.0,"window_minutes":10080,"plan_type":"pro"}
{"timestamp_utc":"2026-10-17T15:46:08.268Z","session":"session-016","workload":"workload-06","model":"gpt-6-astra","reasoning_effort":"ultra","usage_delta":{"input_tokens":206530,"cached_input_tokens":205312,"cache_write_input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":149,"reasoning_output_tokens":73,"total_tokens":206679},"last_input_tokens":206530,"context_window":258400,"weekly_used_percent":91.0,"window_minutes":10080,"plan_type":"pro"}
{"timestamp_utc":"2026-10-17T15:46:14.646Z","session":"session-016","workload":"workload-06","model":"gpt-6-astra","reasoning_effort":"ultra","usage_delta":{"input_tokens":209197,"cached_input_tokens":206464,"cache_write_input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":336,"reasoning_output_tokens":212,"total_tokens":209533},"last_input_tokens":209197,"context_window":258400,"weekly_used_percent":91.0,"window_minutes":10080,"plan_type":"pro"}
```

## Full evidence package available

A sanitized 1.4 MB ZIP has been prepared locally with all 50,204 positive usage increments, the 293-row session summary, aggregate totals, a standard-library verification script and SHA-256 checksums. The ZIP is not attached to this issue yet; it can be provided through an agreed upload channel. No raw private rollouts need to be shared.

Archive SHA-256: `81b9439c6bdc2f8f210f7487c724c70a818b5999d02e85dc31e8b1a60c7bd08a`

Verification result:

```text
PASS: 50,204 increments, 293 sessions, 8,861,733,667 total tokens
```

## Related issue

Related investigation: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/44884

This report provides an independent macOS desktop dataset with a fixed 36-hour window and sanitized evidence. Please consolidate with #44884 if that is the preferred tracking issue.



## Source audit findings

Inspected public source at `rust-v0.163.0-alpha.10.2` (`4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4`), with the compaction path also checked at `rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2` (`740e5af33c71225640e0c1c1555c514c2c93ab74`). These versions occur in local session metadata; metadata alone does not establish which binary handled every resumed request.

### Concrete reporting inconsistency

The per-response ledger contains 50,465 distinct response IDs and 8,949,499,238 tokens. The legacy `token_count.info.total_token_usage` increments contain 50,204 increments and 8,861,733,667 tokens. Zero repeated response IDs were found across the full dataset.

Of the difference, 260 response IDs match installed compactions, totaling 87,636,109 tokens. One further response contributes 129,462 tokens.

The code records [compaction completion in the per-response ledger](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/compact_remote_v2.rs#L428-L447), then [records its rollout-budget usage](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/compact_remote_v2_installation.rs#L185-L190) and [recomputes context usage](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/compact_remote_v2_installation.rs#L277-L280). It does not apply the same cumulative token-info update as ordinary sampling. Please confirm whether this omission from the legacy counter is intentional and which user-facing totals are affected.

### Source-supported amplification mechanism

- [Each sampling step constructs input from retained history](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/session/turn.rs#L553-L558)
- [Default compaction threshold is 90% of context capacity](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/protocol/src/openai_models.rs#L529-L539), permitting many costly steps below the threshold
- [`followup_task` triggers another turn](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents_v2/followup_task.rs#L33-L49); the concurrency limit does not bound repeated rounds
- [Compaction retains selected agent messages](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/compact_remote_v2.rs#L537-L560), subject to a 10,000-token per-message limit and 64,000-token shared retained-message budget
- [Optional rollout-budget fallback](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/rollout_budget.rs#L47-L66) counts weighted output and uncached input unless server-defined units are supplied; it cannot independently serve as a complete cached-token spending cap

These are source-supported mechanisms and an accounting inconsistency, not proof of duplicate billing. The main amplification still needs engineering investigation; changing concurrency alone cannot prevent it. A second sanitized per-response evidence file is available, alongside the original counter-based dataset.



## Installed app inspection and offline concurrency reproducer

The installed app is version `26.1013.40934` (build `20770`), bundling native `codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2`. Its compiled desktop JavaScript was unpacked read-only, and the native ARM64 admission functions were disassembled and compared with the matching public source tag. Runtime SHA-256: `1afb28c01d7d49e892bd75f11076b10f1451e34e0ee308a95e5ab7f69f9c84fe`.

A separate concurrency defect is reproducible: `check_turn_admission` checks capacity without reserving it, then `admit_turn` increments the active count later. The source contract explicitly describes this as non-atomic. The shipped machine code likewise has a separate load/compare and later atomic increment.

- [Limiter implementation](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/execution.rs)
- [Admission contract](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/agent/api.rs#L111-L126)
- [Precheck before asynchronous submission](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/codex_thread.rs#L589-L601)
- [Later guard acquisition](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/core/src/tasks/mod.rs#L340-L345)

A standalone Rust reproduction using those same limiter methods (with dependency stubs and visibility adjustment only) synchronizes two threads after their checks. Both then acquire guards at a configured limit of one:

```text
configured_limit=1 concurrent_admitted=2 per_thread_observations=[2, 2]
REPRODUCED: separate check and increment admits two workers at a limit of one
```

This test performs no network requests or model inference. Atomic permit reservation would close that race.

**This race has not been shown to cause this incident.** The completed-turn history has a peak of 30 overlapping subagent turns in the largest workload, under the configured limit of 40. It is a separate defect found while investigating.

A new classification of the same response ledger finds **11,087 responses issuing only coordination tools, totaling 1,912,871,075 tokens (21.37%)**. Other explicit-tool responses total 6,567,145,729 tokens; responses without an explicit tool call total 469,482,434 tokens. These categories describe observed output calls, not provider billing categories or a claim that every token was unnecessary.

One coordinator ran 1,860 recorded responses in just two turns. Of its 529 waits, 135 returned within one second and 373 within ten seconds. Fresh messages can legitimately wake waits; this is evidence of frequent coordination, not proof of a broken timer.

The incident's main measured mechanism remains repeated tool/coordination steps carrying large retained histories. A single billing, scheduler or memory-corruption defect has not been established as the primary cause. The offline reproducer and additional sanitized profiling data are prepared for maintainers.


## Further investigation: goal accounting excludes billed cached input

The matching source and installed ARM64 binary expose a cost-control gap relevant to this incident. The goal token metric excludes cached input, while Codex's published credit rate for cached input is nonzero. This is intentional in the source's tests, so the engineering question is whether these budget semantics and their presentation are appropriate for billed autonomous work, rather than whether the subtraction is an accidental typo.

At the installed runtime's matching commit, [goal_token_delta_for_usage](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/ext/goal/src/accounting.rs#L570-L575) computes:

```rust
usage.input_tokens
    .saturating_sub(usage.cached_input_tokens)
    .saturating_add(usage.output_tokens.max(0))
```

An offline Rust harness includes this entire upstream accounting file unchanged, with external dependency type stubs. It makes no model/API requests. Results:

```text
per_response: recorded_total=200100 cached_input=200000 goal_budget_count=100
1000_responses: recorded_total=200100000 goal_budget_count=100000
1000_successful_wait_only_turns: empty_response_guard_never_trips
control: truly_empty_turns_trip_guard_at_3
```

The installed `GoalAccountingState::progress_snapshot` disassembly has the corresponding subtraction and addition at `0x1069cf250` and `0x1069cf264`.

The wait-only test establishes the scope of the empty-response safeguard, not a full desktop reproduction: [record_tool_outcome](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/ext/goal/src/accounting.rs#L121-L145) resets the empty-turn streak and marks activity even for successful waits. The safeguard does not measure objective progress. The within-turn sampling loop also continues for tool follow-ups or pending input; one incident coordinator made 1,860 responses in only two turns.

### Matching incident evidence

- Fuller ledger: **8,949,499,238** tokens.
- Cached input: **8,788,141,824**, or **98.197%** of that total.
- Non-cached input plus output: **161,357,414**. Applying the goal formula to all recorded responses would exclude the other 98.197%; this is a metric comparison, not the actual combined goal counter.
- **7,233,111,675** tokens, approximately **80.82%**, were already on Sol 6.1 Low, attributed using the last recorded turn context. A cheaper default alone does not fix the request volume or retained-history amplification.
- One research goal reported `tokensUsed=72,457,032`. In its approximate active interval (2026-10-18 04:38:26 through 08:02:15 UTC), the root and descendants recorded **4,136,902,089** total tokens, of which **4,063,375,104** were cached input.
- The legacy usage path in that interval yields **72,455,823** non-cached input plus output, only 1,209 below the reported goal count. Goal timestamps are second-resolution, so this is not an exact response-level reconciliation. It supports the cache exclusion, and does not support a claim that all descendant usage was missing.

**Causal limit:** the inspected creation calls for the three large goals omitted `token_budget`, and goal reports returned `remainingTokens=null`. The user requested continued overnight work without specifying a token ceiling. Therefore, this incident does not demonstrate violation of a configured goal budget. It demonstrates sustained autonomous work without a spending ceiling, and a goal accounting metric that would not represent all priced usage even if a token budget were configured.

[Current published Codex pricing](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing) assigns nonzero cached-input credit rates. This does not prove incorrect billing or imply cached and uncached input have the same price. The [official Goals guide](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/codex/using_goals_in_codex) describes budget-limited continuation but does not define cached-input exclusion.

Please investigate a cost-aware budget shared across the root and descendants, including cached input and compaction; explicit handling of unbudgeted unattended goals; accurate labels for goal-budget units versus total tokens and billed credits; and repeated waiting/status/retry loops that do not advance the objective. Reconcile the response ledger against private billing records separately.

A sanitized v4 package is prepared locally with the unchanged upstream accounting source, license, portable Rust harness, output, minimal installed-binary disassembly, aggregates and checksums. It contains no prompts, account IDs, credentials or private project contents. The package has not been uploaded to this issue.


## Focused runtime safeguard follow-up

Implementation proposal: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/55180

That companion issue covers pre-request budget reservation shared by the root and descendants, complete spending units, and exhaustion/recovery behavior. The incident evidence, billing reconciliation request, reporting discrepancy and separate concurrency race remain in this report. This is a companion relationship, not a claim that the proposed safeguard proves the incident's root cause.

Source-reference correction: the earlier references used annotated release-tag object hashes as commit identifiers. The source links above now use the underlying commits: `4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4` for `rust-v0.163.0-alpha.10.2`, and `740e5af33c71225640e0c1c1555c514c2c93ab74` for `rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2`. items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.40934

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Team

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

I'm testing app-provided tools in Codex Desktop using the Bits & Bolts Remote MCP App.

The app registers five tools using `app.registerTool()` from `@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps`:

- `read_view`
- `open_part`
- `configure_view`
- `rotate_geometry`
- `save_file`

The MCP App loads successfully, and its UI works as expected. However, none of these app-provided tools are discoverable or callable by the model.

When I ask Codex to list the available tools, it only recognizes server-side MCP tools such as `cad.library`, `cad.search`, and `cad.configureView`.

The app-provided tools registered inside the iframe are not exposed to the model.

This prevents the model from directly interacting with the MCP App's UI state, which is one of the key capabilities of app-provided tools.

It is unclear whether this is an unsupported feature in Codex Desktop or a bug in the host's MCP Apps implementation.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Feedback ID: 7ae2de40-6b33-4d3c-9dbc-28668620edea

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex Desktop should support discovering and invoking app-provided tools registered by MCP Apps.

Specifically:

1. When an MCP App declares the `tools` capability, the host should recognize it during initialization.
2. The host should discover app-provided tools by sending `tools/list` to the MCP App.
3. The discovered tools should become available to the model alongside server-side MCP tools.
4. When the model invokes an app-provided tool, the host should forward the request to the MCP App using `tools/call`.
5. The MCP App should execute the registered handler and return the result to the model.

For example, when the Bits & Bolts viewer is open, the model should be able to invoke `read_view` to inspect the current UI state or `configure_view` to change the camera and rendering settings.

This would enable the model to interact directly with the state of a running MCP App without requiring developers to duplicate client-side functionality as server-side MCP tools.

### Additional information

### Related issue

A similar issue has already been reported in the MCP Extensions repository:

https://github.com/openai/mcp-extensions/issues/36

I'm reporting this here as well because the behavior appears to be related to Codex Desktop's host-side implementation rather than the MCP App itself.

### MCP Apps specification

The MCP Apps specification defines the mechanism for exposing app-provided tools through `tools/list` and `tools/call`.

https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/draft/apps.mdx

### Questions

- Does Codex Desktop currently support app-provided tools?
- If so, is there a specific capability or configuration required to enable them?
- If not, is support planned for a future release?

App-provided tools are particularly important for building agentic user interfaces where the model can inspect and manipulate application state directly.

For example, developers could expose form interactions, selections, navigation, and other UI operations without duplicating the same functionality on the MCP server.

items.title: [macOS][Chrome Browser Use] Auth0 page loading stalls with paused-document-response guard; Cancel reportedly releases loading

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary

Pages in an authenticated web application intermittently stop progressing while ChatGPT Chrome browser control is active. The user reports that clicking **Cancel** in Chrome's “ChatGPT started debugging this browser” banner immediately allows the page to load.

A separate diagnostic tab reproduced delayed loading and a rejection from the supported CDP interface:

```text
Raw CDP is unavailable while Browser Use is resolving a paused document response.
```

Buffered events included `Fetch.requestPaused` for Auth0 `/authorize` Document responses (HTTP 200 and 302). The tab later progressed to the authenticated application layout without this diagnostic session cancelling browser control; full inbox loading was not verified.

Related: #53154, especially [the October 17 Document-response diagnostics](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/53154#issuecomment-6229601691) and [the October 16 Network.enable rejection](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/53154#issuecomment-6206360881). This report concerns page-loading delays during authentication; the original issue's URL-safety refusal was **not** observed here, and a shared root cause is unconfirmed.

## What version of the Codex App are you using?

ChatGPT desktop **26.1013.40934**, build **20770**, production channel, bundle identifier `com.openai.codex`. Verified from installed app metadata and the desktop update-check tool. The updater reported `up_to_date` for its configured channel.

- Google Chrome installed and running: **155.0.8059.80**
- ChatGPT Chrome extension: **1.26.1005.11759**, enabled, verified in Chrome's Extensions UI
- Extension ID: `hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg`
- The official Chrome Web Store listed the same extension version, updated October 15, 2026
- Bundled Computer Use plugin directory version: **26.1013.40934**

## What subscription do you have?

Not collected during this diagnosis.

## What platform is your computer?

macOS **27.0.1**, build **26A434**; 64 GiB RAM.

Observed October 18, 2026, evening, America/Los_Angeles.

## What issue are you seeing?

In a fresh, separately created diagnostic tab, the Dhisana Signal Monitoring route initially rendered only the application shell/header and failed to promptly load protected content. A simple public page had loaded successfully through the same official Chrome connection.

The supported `Network.enable` probe was rejected with the paused-document-response error above. A reload queued after that command did **not** run.

The supported read-only event API returned these retained events, with authentication query values and headers omitted:

| Event | Resource type | Host/path | HTTP status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Fetch.requestPaused` | `Document` | `login-agent.dhisana.ai/authorize` | 200 |
| `Fetch.requestPaused` | `Document` | `login-agent.dhisana.ai/authorize` | 302 |

Local frontend configuration uses Auth0 and authentication-gated routes, consistent with a page remaining partially rendered while sign-in initialization is incomplete.

## What steps can reproduce the bug?

The failure is intermittent; this is an observed sequence, not a deterministic minimal reproducer.

1. Use the official ChatGPT Chrome extension with an existing signed-in Chrome profile.
2. Open an authenticated application page that initializes an Auth0 session.
3. With browser control active, observe the application shell/header while protected content is delayed.
4. Attempt a supported read-only network diagnostic through the tab's advertised CDP capability.
5. Observe the paused-document-response rejection above.
6. Read retained loading events through the documented event API; in this reproduction they included Auth0 `/authorize` Document responses.
7. The user reports that pressing **Cancel** on Chrome's debugging banner releases loading. This global cancellation was not repeated in the diagnostic session because other browser tasks were active.

## What is the expected behavior?

Authentication and page loading should complete normally while browser control is active, or an actionable, bounded error/approval state should explain why progress is blocked. A supported recovery should preserve other active tabs/tasks and applicable security controls.

## Evidence limits and investigation request

- The event buffer reported `truncated: true`; it is not a complete navigation trace.
- A retained `Fetch.requestPaused` event does not prove that the same request remained outstanding at the guard rejection. Matching continuation/release completion and the provider's pending set were not captured.
- Installed browser-service source shows the error is raised when `hasOwnedPausedResponses(tab)` is true. That identifies the guard condition, not the underlying reason or a proven faulty code path.
- The page later made progress without this diagnostic session cancelling control. That is not a demonstrated permanent recovery, and external interaction from concurrent sessions was not isolated.
- Memory pressure looked normal in the sampled interval; extension errors shown in Chrome concerned favicon images on another site. Neither observation proves or excludes every intermittent cause.
- Chrome-profile scan `EPERM` warnings and in-app-browser route/frame warnings were also present, but no causal link to this Chrome stall was established.
- No private account/record identifiers, auth query values, cookies, tokens, full URLs, screenshots, raw logs, or session transcripts are included.

Please investigate Document-response continuation/cleanup during Auth0 initialization and redirects, correlate the guard with actual pending request/frame state, and provide a supported recovery or fixed release. This report does not request disabling or bypassing safeguards.

## Diagnostic report

The full reviewed text report is included inline below so it remains available with the issue.

<details>
<summary>chrome-loading-diagnosis.txt</summary>

```text
Chrome loading diagnosis — October 18, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

Verified versions
- Google Chrome installed and running: 155.0.8059.80.
- ChatGPT desktop: 26.1013.40934, build 20770, production channel.
- Desktop update check: up_to_date for the configured release channel.
- ChatGPT Chrome extension: 1.26.1005.11759, enabled.
- Extension ID: hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg.
- Chrome Web Store lists the same extension version, updated October 15, 2026.
- macOS: 27.0.1, build 26A434.

Observed reproduction
1. Browser inventory and a new simple public page worked through the official
   ChatGPT Chrome connection.
2. In a separate agent-created tab, the affected Dhisana Signal Monitoring route
   initially rendered only the shell/header and did not promptly finish loading.
3. The supported CDP Network.enable diagnostic returned:
   "Raw CDP is unavailable while Browser Use is resolving a paused document response."
   The command was rejected; its subsequent reload did not execute.
4. Read-only buffered events contained Fetch.requestPaused for Document responses
   from login-agent.dhisana.ai/authorize, with HTTP statuses 200 and 302.
   Authentication query values, headers, cookies and tokens were not printed.
   The event buffer was truncated, so it is not a complete navigation trace.
5. A later observation showed the authenticated Signal Monitoring layout and
   "Loading review inbox...". The page made progress without this diagnostic
   session cancelling browser control. Full inbox completion was not verified.
6. The isolated browser test tab was closed. No existing work tab was reloaded.

Assessment
The strongest evidence points to delayed or stuck document-response interception
in the ChatGPT Browser Use path during Dhisana authentication. The local source
confirms the diagnostic message is raised when Browser Use tracks owned paused
document responses. Local frontend configuration uses Auth0 and route guards
that wait for authentication, which is consistent with the partially rendered UI.

The exact reason the response remains held is not established. A browser/runtime
interaction, response-continuation failure or stale bookkeeping still needs
engineering investigation. The observations do not prove a general macOS fault,
a broken Dhisana backend, an extension conflict, or a particular security decision.
The user's Cancel-to-resume observation was reported by the user and was not
repeated globally, to avoid interrupting other active browser tasks.

Other findings
- Memory-pressure query reported 75% system-wide memory free on a 64 GiB Mac.
  No runaway multi-gigabyte Chrome renderer was observed in the sampled processes.
  This snapshot cannot rule out an intermittent memory problem.
- Extension Errors showed two favicon image errors on another site. No direct
  relation to the Dhisana loading issue was established.
- Desktop logs contain Chrome-profile scan EPERM warnings and in-app-browser
  route/frame warnings. These are not established causes of this Chrome stall.
- Chrome profile files were protected by macOS; no permissions were broadened.
- No extension settings, security controls, application code or updates were changed.
- The native Extensions diagnostics tab may remain open; cleanup was interrupted
  by the user changing Chrome, so further native UI actions were stopped.

Suggested recovery
Finish active browser tasks, then fully quit and reopen Chrome and ChatGPT and
retry one new browser task. If the problem persists, use /feedback with this
diagnosis and reference the related report below. Manual Cancel remains the
user-observed temporary workaround, but disconnects active browser control.
No permanent fixed version was verified. Do not infer that broader permissions
or disabling safeguards are necessary.

Sources
Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/chatgpt/hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg
Related macOS report, including the same paused-document diagnostic:
https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/53154
Official browser extension recovery guidance:
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/chrome-extension#troubleshooting
```

</details>

items.body:
### Observed behavior

On 2026-10-16, Windows Codex CLI `0.163.0-alpha.10.2` failed to initialize an OAuth-protected enterprise MCP connection. The same failure was reproduced on two computers and during an independent CLI login-discovery check, before the browser authorization step.

The MCP resource, protected-resource metadata and authorization server use the same HTTPS origin on an RFC1918 IPv4 address. Normal HTTPS requests validate the certificate successfully; health and both discovery documents return HTTP 200 with valid JSON. The advertised authorization-server URL agrees with its metadata issuer.

Sanitized errors:

```text
rejecting authorization server metadata URL `https://<private-ip>:<port>/`
failed to resolve OAuth metadata before using stored credentials
protected resource metadata ... names authorization servers ...,
but none published usable metadata
```

### Reproduction

1. Configure an OAuth MCP server at a private IPv4 HTTPS origin, with a certificate trusted by the Windows user.
2. Publish same-origin protected-resource metadata with `resource` and `authorization_servers`, and authorization-server metadata with matching `issuer`, authorization/token/registration endpoints and S256 PKCE support.
3. Connect through native Codex HTTP MCP OAuth using stored credentials, or attempt CLI OAuth login discovery.
4. Observe discovery rejection before tools become available.

### Version analysis — source comparison, not runtime A/B testing

- Codex `0.162.1` and `0.163.0-alpha.6` pin rmcp 3.3.0.
- `0.163.0-alpha.8` pins rmcp 3.5.1, following [Codex #52972](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/52972).
- [rust-sdk #935](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk/pull/935) introduced the private authorization-server URL check.
- [rust-sdk #1264](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk/pull/1264) changed an unusable advertised authorization-server result from fallback to an error. This appears to explain the failure after the dependency upgrade.
- Source inspection on 2026-10-19 found the same relevant rejection/error paths in the dependencies used by `0.163.0` and `0.164.0-alpha.3`. Those releases and a rollback to `0.162.1` have NOT been runtime-tested for this report.

### Expected behavior / requested clarification

Please confirm a supported secure configuration for an explicitly trusted, same-origin enterprise private-IP OAuth authorization server, or provide narrowly scoped support with appropriate trust controls. Please preserve SSRF protections for untrusted discovery targets.

This report concerns the native HTTP MCP OAuth path. It contains no credentials, real network addresses, tenant/application identifiers, account details, conversation IDs, private hostnames, or raw diagnostic attachments.

labels.name: bug

labels.name: model-behavior

labels.name: windows-os

labels.name: tool-calls

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Incident rollout: bundled CLI 0.162.0-alpha.17.2, originator Codex Desktop. Currently installed Windows package: OpenAI.Codex 26.1013.4894.0; the incident-time About-dialog version was not independently captured.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT-authenticated Codex Desktop; exact subscription tier not specified in this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Pro x64, 10.0.26200; WSL2 Ubuntu-24.04. Command path: PowerShell -> wsl.exe -> /bin/bash -lc -> Python 3.12.

### What issue are you seeing?

## Summary

On 18 October 2026, a Codex Desktop agent using **gpt-6-luna** cleared the contents of my Windows project workspace, `D:\Opencode\M_easytier`, while preparing a temporary Python environment for project tests. I had not asked it to delete the project.

The agent generated a `python -m venv --clear` command intended for a directory under `/tmp`. Surviving process evidence shows that its target argument had become an empty string by the time the cross-shell command was running. The command had been launched with the project directory as its working directory. Source files, handoff documents and test records subsequently disappeared.

**The affected directory was the project workspace itself, not my home directory.** This is important: protecting only paths outside the workspace would not prevent this incident.

## Observed evidence

- The preserved incident rollout identifies model `gpt-6-luna`, bundled CLI `0.162.0-alpha.17.2`, `approval_policy=never`, and `sandbox_policy.type=danger-full-access`. This report does not allege a sandbox escape.
- At **2026-10-17 23:40:05 UTC / 2026-10-18 07:40:05 UTC+8**, the agent launched a PowerShell wrapper that passed a multiline script to `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-24.04 -- /bin/bash -lc $script`. The tool working directory was `D:\Opencode\M_easytier`.
- At **23:40:47 UTC**, a process listing captured the effective command fragment below. This is a historical excerpt, **not a command to execute**:

```text
/usr/bin/python3.12 -m venv --clear --copies --system-site-packages ""
test -x "/bin/python"
```

- At **23:41:25 UTC**, the next attempt failed because the project test runner no longer existed. A subsequent check reported `pwd=/mnt/d/Opencode/M_easytier` and confirmed the missing project file.
- The agent subsequently acknowledged that an empty/wrong path passed to `venv --clear` had cleared the project contents.

The empty argument and missing files are recorded observations. The explanation that Python resolved the empty target against the working directory is the supported deletion mechanism; I am not claiming to have a complete filesystem syscall trace.

## Impact

This project represented roughly two weeks of development, including a Windows client, a shared Rust networking core for Windows/Linux, a Web backend/frontend, deployment documents and acceptance-test automation. Before the incident, the recorded progress was Stage A 39/39 and Stage B 190/207 subtests.

An independent source tree, remote binaries and surviving transcripts allowed substantial recovery, so I am **not** claiming that every two-week-old result is permanently lost. However, some original runners, documents and raw evidence could not be fully recovered. Recovery and re-establishing the real Hub/Windows test chain have already consumed more than a day. This has been a severe loss of work and trust.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

## Historical triggering sequence (do not run on a real workspace)

1. Codex was continuing project testing in a Windows workspace mapped into WSL at `/mnt/d/Opencode/M_easytier`.
2. It attempted to prepare a temporary Python virtual environment under `/tmp/stageb-b11-r164-py312`.
3. Its generated Bash script assigned `VENV` and then invoked `venv --clear` with `"$VENV"`. PowerShell passed that script through `wsl.exe` to `bash -lc`.
4. The observed running command contained `""` in place of the intended environment path, and later references had become `/bin/python`.
5. Project contents disappeared and the next runner launch failed with “No such file or directory”.

I have not rerun the destructive command to obtain a deterministic reproducer. Please investigate argument preservation/expansion across the Windows/WSL wrapper and safeguards for destructive environment initialization. Any engineering reproduction should use a disposable fixture containing only synthetic marker files.

The relevant rollout excerpts and session identifier are preserved and can be provided through an appropriate private support channel after redaction. Raw transcripts are not attached publicly because they also contain unrelated private project data.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Preparing a temporary environment must not clear an existing project/source directory.
- Empty, unset or malformed target arguments must fail before any destructive operation.
- Treat `venv --clear` and similar indirect deletion operations as destructive, even when no `rm` or `Remove-Item` appears.
- Validate the final canonical target after cross-shell argument handling, against the intended disposable environment directory; reject the current working directory and project/source roots.
- If clearing an existing directory is genuinely necessary, show its resolved path and destructive effect and obtain explicit, scoped human approval. General development/testing access is not an instruction to erase source and evidence.
- Please investigate model/tooling safeguards for workspace destruction under full-access configurations, as well as wrapper quoting. Workspace-write permission alone would still include the directory harmed here.

### Additional information

## Related reports

- #42875 reports macOS home-directory data loss while GPT-5.6 Sol sessions were running.
- #38312 and #19202 also discuss unintended deletion of user/project files.

I am linking these as related data-loss reports, not asserting an identical implementation defect. This incident has a different model/platform and a concrete `venv --clear` / empty-target command trail. The central similarity is that temporary-environment work caused destructive deletion of valuable existing user data.

Please preserve relevant server-side records and investigate why this dangerous operation was generated and allowed to reach the project directory. I would appreciate concrete mitigations for destructive commands hidden inside environment setup, and confirmation whether the existing deletion protections cover workspace/source roots as well as home directories.

中文摘要：2026年10月18日，Codex在准备测试环境时，通过PowerShell/WSL运行venv --clear，目标参数在实际进程中变成空字符串，导致Windows项目工作目录被清空。主要源码和成品虽已部分恢复，但部分交接文档、验收脚本和原始记录未完整找回；恢复及重建测试链路已耗费超过一天。受损的是工作目录，不是用户主目录。
